title: The Dynamics of Spectral Hands Coordination and Hayekian Time
affiliations: George Mason University, College of Science

detail.title: The Dynamics of Spectral Hands Coordination and Hayekian Time

declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A

detail.abstract:
This paper extends Friedrich A. Hayek’s research program by interpreting economic coordination as a problem of ordering under constraint rather than optimization. Building on Hayek’s critique of equilibrium formalism and his later work in The
Sensory Order, the paper treats machines not as metaphors but as epistemic coordination devices that enforce these constraints on order. Using the historical development of railroad signaling and administration as a concrete case, the paper places Hayek in dialogue with Alfred Chandler’s account of managerial coordination, Herbert Simon’s ideas of bounded rationality and near decomposability, and Ronald Coase’s analysis of firm boundaries. These cases illustrate how coordination problems are solved through machine-enforced ordering rather than centralized calculation or price adjustment alone. To make this perspective precise, the paper introduces mathematical tools drawn from order theory, distributed systems, and graph theory, not to optimize outcomes but to clarify the limits and structure of feasible coordination. The result is a Hayekian framework for modeling markets, firms, and infrastructures as computational systems that coordinate dispersed knowledge without omniscience. It is intended as generative of future work.

title: How Aggregation Works – An Exact Aggregation-Disaggregation Method for a Class of Mixed-Integer Linear Programs
affiliations: Beijing Jiaotong University, University of Twente and Beijing Jiaotong University

detail.title: How Aggregation Works – An Exact Aggregation-Disaggregation Method for a Class of Mixed-Integer Linear Programs
detail.abstract: Although aggregating items such as commodities, vehicles, or resources into groups is widely used in planning and operations, the structural conditions under which aggregation is exact have not been systematically characterized. In this paper, we provide a mathematical foundation for aggregation techniques using mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs). Specifically, we prove that a class of MILPs can be solved to optimality by aggregating certain sets of variables and constraints, solving a smaller model with fewer symmetries and the same linear relaxation value, and then disaggregating the solution in polynomial time. The method applies to MILPs with block-diagonal and coupling constraints in which variable vectors share identical coefficients in the objective and coupling constraints. The exactness of the aggregation holds when (i) the diagonal blocks are identical totally unimodular matrices with proportional right-hand sides, or (ii) their constraints represent the balance of network flows with same source or same sink. This aggregation-disaggregation method has both theoretical and computational value. On the theoretical side, it formalizes the fundamental mechanisms underlying existing aggregation techniques, extends and/or strengthens the theory and applicability of several structure-based methods for MILPs, and establishes polynomial-time solvability for a class of MILPs. Computationally, we evaluate the method on three well-known optimization problems: service network design, vehicle scheduling, and hierarchical interval scheduling. Using Gurobi, we show that, compared to directly solving the original formulations, our method solves more instances to optimality and achieves average speedups of over 10, 2500, and 1000 times, respectively, for the three problems.

title: Trade Secrecy &The Government's Right To Repair
affiliations: University of Virginia School of Law and University of Virginia School of Law

detail.title: Trade Secrecy &The Government's Right To Repair

publicationDetails.detailsText: Virginia Public Law and Legal Theory Research Paper No 12-2026
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Virginia Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: Virginia Journal of Law and Technology, Forthcoming

detail.abstract: The Department of Defense's struggles to obtain repair rights from private contractors have reached crisis levels, with military personnel facing critical equipment delays while contractors fear losing valuable trade secrets. The 2025 bipartisan "Warrior Right to Repair Act" attempts to address this problem but has generated fierce opposition from industry groups. This Paper provides the first scholarly analysis of how trade secrecy law shapes the government's perceived inability to obtain intellectual property rights from defense contractors. We demonstrate that the crisis stems not from irreconcilable legal conflicts, but from a failure to apply existing trade secret mechanisms for managed disclosure that commonly facilitate business-to-business transactions in the private sector. While the FAR appears to promise the government sufficient control over repair rights, in practice both sides distrust the current framework. By analyzing how trade secrecy's built-in flexibility for balancing proprietary protection with necessary disclosure could work in procurement contexts, we propose reconceptualizing these transactions toward a "who-whatwhy" transaction-based framework that accounts for the government's special needs while preserving legitimate contractor protections. This reframing reveals that the tools already exist to resolve right-to-repair tensions in defense contracting and can be operationalized through tailored contract-by-contract negotiation.

title: Lost in Translation? Injunctions and Patent Enforcement in a Transatlantic Perspective
affiliations: Università degli Studi della Basilicata

detail.title: Lost in Translation? Injunctions and Patent Enforcement in a Transatlantic Perspective

declarations.funderStatement: The study has been conducted as part of the research activities promoted by the Research Network for Digital Ecosystem, Economic Policy and Innovation (Deep-In Network).

detail.abstract: As the European Directive on the Enforcement of Intellectual Property Rights (IPRED) marked the twentieth anniversary of its adoption, renewed calls have emerged for its revision, aimed at fostering a more effective application of the principle of proportionality in patent enforcement. Proponents of reform argue that injunctive relief continues to be granted in an overly automatic manner and should therefore be subject to greater restraint. To this end, it has been suggested that valuable guidance may be drawn from the U.S. legal landscape and, in particular, from the framework articulated by the U.S. Supreme Court in eBay v. MercExchange. Against this background, the paper critically examines these reform proposals, arguing that they appear to rest on the same arguments that underpinned the highly controversial regulatory proposal on standard essential patents (SEPs), and questioning the purported alignment between the European and the U.S. approaches to patent enforcement.

title: Innovative Firms Unveiled: Economic and Financial Insights from Italian Start-Ups
affiliations: Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy, Organization for Economic Co-Operation and Development (OECD), Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: Innovative Firms Unveiled: Economic and Financial Insights from Italian Start-Ups

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 967
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This study analyzes the economic and financial characteristics of innovative firms in Italy from 2010 to 2024, focusing on two key groups: innovative start-ups as defined by the Italian ‘Start-up Act’ (INN-SUs) and venture capital-backed start-ups (VCB-SUs). Both groups are then compared with a broader group of young, limited liability companies (OTH-SUs). Despite representing a small share of the start-up population (2.2 per cent and 0.2 per cent, respectively), INN-SUs and VCB-SUs are disproportionately active in innovation, particularly in patenting. Their ownership structures are more diversified, with younger, predominantly male investors often located outside the firm’s province. While initially smaller in revenues and employment, innovative firms exhibit higher asset intensity and a more robust long-term growth trajectory. Notably, VCB-SUs experience significant post-investment expansion, highlighting the role of venture capital in easing financial constraints and providing strategic support. The findings suggest that regulatory and market-based definitions of innovation capture complementary dimensions of entrepreneurial potential, with policy frameworks enabling broader access and VC investments signalling high-growth prospects.

title:
Open-Loop Cognition and the Architecture of Identity Operations 
Why Representation is not Consciousness
affiliations: Epistria

detail.title:
Open-Loop Cognition and the Architecture of Identity Operations 
Why Representation is not Consciousness
detail.abstract: Current frameworks for understanding cognition routinely distinguish non-representational regulation from conscious experience, yet lack a stable term for the regime between them: representational operations that are self-referential but not recursively closed. This paper introduces Open-Loop Cognition as that missing category. Open-loop cognition consists of representational, self-referential identity operations that evaluate trajectories and model futures without recursive closure. In this regime, identity may be referenced, evaluated, or simulated, but not constituted or enforced. The concept explains a persistent puzzle: why systems capable of sophisticated self-modeling remain systematically vulnerable to capture and manipulation. The answer is architectural. Open-loop cognition supports self-reference without self-ratification—the model does not bind the modeler. This paper defines the regime, specifies its scalar properties, characterizes its vulnerability profile, and distinguishes it from both non-representational regulation (autoteria, orthesis) and consciousness (recursive closure). The contribution is primarily definitional: naming a regime that existing vocabularies conflate or omit.

title: The Role of Domestic Institutional and Retail Investors in Stabilizing the Indian Stock Market Amid Foreign Portfolio Outflows: Evidence from 2020-2025
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Role of Domestic Institutional and Retail Investors in Stabilizing the Indian Stock Market Amid Foreign Portfolio Outflows: Evidence from 2020-2025
detail.abstract: This paper examines the pivotal role of domestic institutional investors (DIIs) and retail investors in stabilizing the Indian equity market during a period of unprecedented foreign portfolio investor (FPI) outflows between 2020 and 2025. Using daily flow data from NSE/BSE, NSDL reports, and market indices, the study employs regression analysis, Granger causality tests, and event study methodology to assess the relationship between investor category flows and market returns/volatility. The empirical findings reveal that 2025 witnessed the highest-ever FPI exodus of ₹1.58 lakh crore, yet the Nifty 50 and Sensex delivered modest gains of approximately 10% and 8-9% respectively, supported by record DII inflows of ₹7.7 lakh crore and sustained retail participation through systematic investment plans. Regression results demonstrate that DII flows exhibit a strong positive association with index stability and significantly reduce volatility during FPI withdrawal phases, while retail SIP contributions-which tripled from ₹1.00 lakh crore in FY20 to ₹2.89 lakh crore in FY25-provide consistent demand that cushions market corrections. The study documents a structural transformation in Indian capital markets, where domestic ownership surpassed foreign holdings for the first time in March 2025, with retail investors controlling 27.4% and DIIs holding 17.82% of NSE-listed companies. These findings have important implications for emerging market policymakers seeking to reduce vulnerability to volatile foreign capital flows while deepening domestic financial participation. The research contributes to literature on institutional trading behavior, market microstructure in emerging economies, and the democratization of equity investment through technological and regulatory reforms.

title: SME Taxation and Compliance Challenges in Emerging Markets
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: SME Taxation and Compliance Challenges in Emerging Markets
detail.abstract: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) play a critical role in emerging markets by driving employment creation, innovation, and inclusive economic growth. Despite their economic significance, tax compliance among SMEs remains persistently low, undermining domestic revenue mobilisation and fiscal sustainability (Waskita & Ashari). Several policy reforms have been introduced across emerging economies to simplify tax systems and broaden the tax base; however, non-compliance continues to pose a major challenge (Bruce-Twum, Nartey). This study conducts a qualitative-conceptual synthesis of existing empirical evidence and policy-oriented literature on SME taxation, compliance behaviour, and administrative mechanisms in emerging markets. Drawing on prior analytical and institutional studies (Judijanto; VALERIAN), the paper integrates insights from taxation theory, compliance cost analysis, and public administration research. The findings reveal that SME tax non-compliance is largely driven by structural tax complexity, high compliance and record-keeping costs, weak enforcement capacity, and inadequate taxpayer education and awareness (Mpofu; Evaluating the Impact of Taxpayer Education on Compliance). These factors interact to discourage voluntary compliance and limit the effectiveness of enforcement-focused reforms. The study concludes that improving SME tax compliance in emerging markets requires an integrated policy framework that combines simplified tax regimes, digital audit trails to enhance financial transparency, and targeted taxpayer education programmes. Such a coordinated approach is essential for strengthening compliance, improving trust in tax authorities, and supporting sustainable economic development (Audit Trails, Financial Transparency).

title: Cybersecurity Risk Management in the Financial Sector: Data Security Challenges in the Era of Remote Working and Service Digitalization
affiliations: Bung Karno University

detail.title: Cybersecurity Risk Management in the Financial Sector: Data Security Challenges in the Era of Remote Working and Service Digitalization
detail.abstract: The advancement of information technology has encouraged the financial sector to undergo significant digital transformation, including the implementation of digital-based financial services and remote working arrangements. Although these developments enhance efficiency and service performance, they also introduce increased cybersecurity risks, particularly concerning data protection and system security. The financial sector is especially vulnerable to cyber threats due to its role in handling sensitive customer information and high-value financial transactions. This paper examines cybersecurity risk management in the financial sector by emphasizing data security challenges associated with remote working and service digitalization. Employing a qualitative literature review approach, this study analyzes various cyber risks such as data breaches, phishing, malware attacks, and system weaknesses, along with strategies to manage and reduce these risks. The findings suggest that effective cybersecurity risk management must be implemented through systematic risk identification and assessment, the application of technical and non-technical safeguards, and continuous improvement of employee awareness. Consequently, robust cybersecurity risk management is crucial to ensure data security, operational stability, and sustained customer trust in the digital environment.

title: The Role of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence in Modern Business Decision-Making
affiliations: Bung Karno University

detail.title: The Role of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence in Modern Business Decision-Making
detail.abstract:
This research aims to advance information technology in business, particularly through Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (AI). Big Data helps companies collect and analyze large amounts of data quickly, while AI processes that data to provide accurate insights.

In the business world, the combination of Big Data and AI plays a crucial role in today's decision-making processes, from strategic planning and consumer behavior analysis to risk management and operational efficiency improvements. With the support of machine learning algorithms and advanced analytics, companies can make decisions faster, more accurately, and based on valid data.

The results of this study show that by using Big Data and AI, Tokopedia can make marketing and operational decisions. Analysis of consumer behavior data enables a more relevant product recommendation system, which increases sales and customer loyalty. Some of Tokopedia's innovations and features that have adopted AI include the Chatbot feature for Tokopedia Care services, Smart Search, Branch Stores, and Quick Recommendations.

title: The Impact of Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Lending on MSMEs' Access to Finance: An Analysis of the Credit Gap
affiliations: Bung Karno University

detail.title: The Impact of Peer-to-Peer (P2P) Lending on MSMEs' Access to Finance: An Analysis of the Credit Gap
detail.abstract:
The limited access of Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) to formal financing remains a persistent challenge in Indonesia, particularly due to stringent banking requirements, limited financial records, and perceived credit risk. These conditions contribute to the emergence of a credit gap that constrains MSME growth and business sustainability. In this context, Peer-to-Peer (P2P) lending has emerged as a digital financing alternative that offers more flexible and accessible funding mechanisms for MSMEs.

This paper aims to examine the role of P2P lending in improving MSMEs’ access to financing and reducing the credit gap. Using a descriptive-analytical approach, the study discusses the concept and characteristics of P2P lending, the financing constraints faced by MSMEs, and the potential contribution of P2P lending in addressing these constraints. The analysis highlights that P2P lending facilitates faster fund disbursement, offers more flexible financing schemes, and expands access to capital for non-bankable MSMEs. However, the paper also identifies several challenges and risks associated with P2P lending, including default risk, data security concerns, limited financial literacy, and regulatory issues.

Overall, this paper concludes that P2P lending has the potential to serve as an alternative financing mechanism that supports financial inclusion and MSME development, provided that its utilization is accompanied by adequate risk awareness, improved financial literacy, and effective regulatory oversight. The findings of this study are expected to contribute to academic discussions on digital finance and provide insights for policymakers and MSME stakeholders in designing more inclusive financing strategies.

title: DFAS-GNAA-CS-01: From Recurrent Institutional Signals to Early-Stage Governance Risk Interpretation: A DFAS Meta-Scientific Case Application (Bahrain as a Bounded Context)
affiliations: Institute of Certified Public Accountant ( ICPAP)

detail.title: DFAS-GNAA-CS-01: From Recurrent Institutional Signals to Early-Stage Governance Risk Interpretation: A DFAS Meta-Scientific Case Application (Bahrain as a Bounded Context)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial, professional, or personal interests that could have influenced the research or its interpretation.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, personal data, or identifiable subjects. No ethics approval or informed consent was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Professional governance systems may appear procedurally stable and formally compliant when assessed through isolated decisions or discrete events. Such assessments, however, risk overlooking early-stage governance fragility that emerges through repetition, omission, and structural persistence over time particularly in small, highly interconnected institutional environments. This case study applies Dynamic Financial Applied Meta-Science (DFAS) as a meta-scientific knowledge-production architecture to examine how recurrent institutional behavior can generate structurally latent governance risk in the absence of explicit violations, misconduct, or non-compliance.

Operating within a methodologically bounded national context, the analysis relies exclusively on previously published DFAS integration outputs rather than raw observations or case-specific data. A structured sequence of DFAS-Signals documenting observable institutional processes is first consolidated into recurrent structural patterns and subsequently translated into aggregated governance risk signals. The case-level application interprets these outputs at the system level while strictly avoiding attribution of responsibility, evaluative judgment, or legal assessment.

The findings demonstrate that governance risk may accumulate through formally acceptable yet structurally invariant configurations, including persistent opacity in evaluation logic, procedural closure without explanatory follow-up, and symbolic variation masking stable decision structures. By treating repetition rather than violation as evidentiary, DFAS enables the detection of pre-failure governance conditions that conventional compliance-, audit-, or incident-based approaches typically fail to capture.

This study contributes methodologically rather than diagnostically. It illustrates DFAS as a pre-theoretical, signal-first architecture that governs how governance-relevant evidence is produced prior to interpretation or theory engagement. Substantively, it advances understanding of how governance risk can emerge quietly through structural persistence and provides empirically grounded feedback for the ongoing refinement of DFAS-GNAA, without validating or redefining the framework itself. The case underscores the value of temporally aware, pattern-based governance analysis in professional systems where legitimacy is sustained through routine rather than rupture.

title: Funding Resilience or Missing the Mark? An Analysis of RRF Allocation and Climate Risk Alignment in Italian Municipalities
affiliations: Gran Sasso Science Institute (GSSI), Università degli Studi di Roma Tre and Roma Tre University

detail.title: Funding Resilience or Missing the Mark? An Analysis of RRF Allocation and Climate Risk Alignment in Italian Municipalities

publicationDetails.detailsText: FEEM Working Paper No. 08-2026
publicationDetails.journalName: FEEM Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Natural hazards are an increasing concern, placing disaster preparedness and mitigation at the forefront of policy agendas. In this context, Italy’s Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP) has allocated €3 billion for explicit disaster prevention, with a primary focus on hydrogeological risks such as floods and landslides. This study evaluates the geographical and thematic distribution of resilience-related funding, examining whether financial resources have been effectively targeted toward municipalities with the highest exposure to environmental hazards. Using a clustering classification, we identify substantial disparities in the allocation of resilience funds, revealing that municipalities with relatively low risk levels often receive disproportionately high funding, while high-risk areas remain underfunded. To explore the underlying drivers of this misalignment, we apply a multinomial logit model to assess the socio-economic and geographic determinants of these funding disparities. Our findings indicate that GDP, macro-regional location, and past disaster occurrences significantly influence whether a municipality falls into a misallocated funding cluster. The misalignment between risk exposure and funding allocation raises questions about the criteria used for distributing adaptation investments and highlights the necessity for a more risk-sensitive and equitable approach.

title: Explainable AI Methods for Autonomous Cloud Orchestration Decisions in FinTech Microservices

detail.title: Explainable AI Methods for Autonomous Cloud Orchestration Decisions in FinTech Microservices
detail.abstract: Efficient cloud resource management in FinTech microservices remains a critical challenge due to the dynamic workload patterns, strict service-level agreements (SLAs), and energy constraints inherent in financial applications (Surisetti, 2025; Dathwal, 2025). This study investigates the integration of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods to enhance autonomous orchestration decisions in cloud environments. We employ reinforcement learning (RL) frameworks to dynamically allocate computing resources while monitoring key performance indicators, including latency, throughput, energy efficiency, and SLA adherence (Kurapati, 2025; Emma, 2024). The methodology emphasizes interpretable decision-making, enabling operators to trace and understand the rationale behind resource allocation choices. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that XAI-guided RL agents achieve significant improvements in operational transparency and resource efficiency without compromising SLA compliance. Moreover, the approach provides actionable insights for auditing and debugging, bridging the gap between autonomous systems and human oversight. These findings underscore the potential of XAI-enhanced orchestration to support trustworthy, scalable, and energy-conscious cloud management in FinTech environments (Gajwani, 2025; Bhatia & Sandiri, 2025). Overall, the study contributes to the growing need for transparent AI-driven cloud solutions that align with both regulatory requirements and high-performance financial computing demands.

title: Corrigibility as a Structural Precondition for Digital Public Infrastructure: A Cybernetic Framework

detail.title: Corrigibility as a Structural Precondition for Digital Public Infrastructure: A Cybernetic Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. This research was conducted independently without financial support from any organization with a stake in the systems evaluated.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a theoretical framework paper and did not involve human participants, patient data, or case studies.

detail.abstract: Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI)-including identity systems, payment rails, data exchanges, and increasingly AI-based services-is being deployed globally at population scale. International definitions from the G20 and United Nations articulate desirable attributes (open, inclusive, accountable) without specifying structural conditions under which these attributes can be verified or enforced. This paper introduces a formal framework for evaluating DPI based on corrigibility: the structural capacity of those affected by a system to detect error, signal harm, and trigger correction without incurring material loss. We derive five necessary tests-EXIT (safe refusal), CODE (legible execution), AUDIT (independent verification), GOVERN (constitutive input), and FORK (credible replacement)-from three independent theoretical traditions: cybernetics (Ashby's Law of Requisite Variety), commons governance (Ostrom's design principles), and free software principles. We prove that failure of any single test disqualifies a system from DPI status and extend the framework to learned systems (AI), where verification shifts from inspecting execution to bounding behavior. The framework is released under CC0 public domain to enable universal adoption.

title: Internal Audit And Albanian SMEs
affiliations: Albanian Institute for Public Affairs, University of Tirana - Faculty of Economics and Albanian University

detail.title: Internal Audit And Albanian SMEs
detail.abstract: Small and medium-sized enterprises have long been recognized as engines of economic growth and development. The impact of small and medium enterprises even in the global economy are very important for increasing employment and reducing poverty. Studies have shown that majority of SMEs die prematurely, before reaching their goals due to poor management resulting from inadequate, weak, uncertain accounting and financial information, as well as the lack of regular auditing and risk management. The purpose of this research is to access the impact of internal audit at Albanian SMEs. The sample for the study consists of 110 entrepreneurs and 80 managers. Primary data for the study were collected by a combination of survey questionnaire and semi-structured interviews. Findings from the study highlight the lack of standard audit system and financial records has been a major obstacle to statutory audit of many SMEs, and by extension negatively affects their performance as they find it difficult to convince stakeholders (creditors, suppliers, tax authorities, etc.), that there was regular supervision by an independent auditor for their business activities. The finding further revealed that this can be eliminated through the adoption of a sound audit system that complies with the Auditing Standards. It has therefore been recommended that SMEs should be encouraged to embrace internal auditing.

title: A Visual Analysis of Hazardous Events in Contract Risk Management
affiliations: Leiden University, Independent, Independent, Leiden University - Leiden Law School and Leiden University - Center for Law and Digital Technologies

detail.title: A Visual Analysis of Hazardous Events in Contract Risk Management

publicationDetails.detailsText: 12th International conference on data science, technology and applications (DATA 2023), 2023, p. 227-234.

detail.abstract: This article proposes a new visual analysis method of hazardous events to be used in contract risk management. We present our research work for the creation of an ontological extension of the Onassis Ontology to manage, analyse and visualise risk data. Onassis is an openly accessible ontology that we earlier designed to structure contract automation data. Onassis and its extension for risk management contribute to the development of trustworthy Intelligent Contracts (iContracts). They allow for the creation of explicit data out of usually implicit contractual information and legal processes on which it is possible to perform cross-referencing analysis with other collections of data. The ontological model that resulted from our study additionally contributes to the disambiguation of the bow-tie method structure, the primary method for analysing and visualising hazardous events. To achieve this, we use the following methodology. We visualise the bow-tie method in an ontology and then investigate the presence of taxonomic ambiguities or even errors in its structure. The results present an enriched version of bow-tie conceptualisation, in which entities and relationships are translated into openly-accessible and ready-to-use ontological terms, whereas risk analysis becomes visible. Nowadays, legal experts act as legal risk mana.

title: AI-Augmented Query Optimization: A Technical Survey of Foundations, Systems, and Open Challenges
affiliations: Bowling Green State University, University of Toledo, , Bowling Green State University and Bowling Green State University

detail.title: AI-Augmented Query Optimization: A Technical Survey of Foundations, Systems, and Open Challenges
detail.abstract: Query optimization has been a cornerstone of database management systems for over four decades, yet traditional cost-based optimizers struggle with complex analytical workloads, userdefined functions, and correlated data distributions. Recent advances in artificial intelligence and machine learning offer a transformative approach: learning optimization strategies from data rather than relying solely on hand-crafted heuristics. This survey provides a comprehensive analysis of AI-augmented query optimization, examining the evolution from rule-based systems to learned components that adapt to workload characteristics and system dynamics. We present a systematic taxonomy of learned optimization approaches spanning four major categories: learned cardinality estimation, learned cost models, reinforcement learning for plan enumeration, and endto-end learned optimizers. Through detailed comparative analysis of systems including Bao, Neo, Lero, and recent LLM-based approaches, we demonstrate that learned optimizers achieve 1.5-3× geometric mean speedups on standard benchmarks while reducing cardinality estimation errors by an order of magnitude. However, challenges remain in generalization, interpretability, training data requirements, and production deployment. We critically examine evaluation methodologies, identifying reproducibility concerns and inconsistent benchmarking practices that hinder progress. Our analysis of integration strategies reveals that hybrid architectures combining traditional and learned components offer the most promising path to production adoption. Finally, we outline future directions including neuro-symbolic optimization, federated learning, transfer learning across databases, and the development of standardized MLOps pipelines. This survey serves as both a comprehensive reference for researchers and a practical guide for practitioners considering AI-augmented optimization in production systems.

detail.abstract: We introduce a series of Epstein-Zhao diagrams that depict how neural transduction theory (NTT) might explain a wide range of mysterious human phenomena. NTT, which is consistent with Darwin’s theory of evolution and with modern, mainstream theories of cosmology, suggests that between 50 and 70,000 years ago, a human infant was born with a brain that acted as a transducer, connecting that individual to a higher intelligence in another dimension. Our conjecture that evolution might produce such a brain – although perhaps quite rarely – is not unreasonable. Just as evolution has produced millions of different species, it has also produced millions of different transducers; the human body is encased from head to toe in transducers, and numerous other unique types of transducers are common in the animal kingdom. Among more than 80 other mysterious phenomena, NTT easily solves Darwin’s uplift problem – that is, it explains how evolution was finally able to produce human-level intelligence – and it also helps us to understand dreams (and why it is so difficult to remember them), unconsciousness (for which no biomarkers have ever been found), genius, schizophrenia, and many other mysterious phenomena, including, we believe, the Fermi Paradox. Moreover, NTT is both falsifiable and empirically testable. We will show how activating simple transduction pathways (simplex or dual-simplex, with varying levels of distortion) might account for 17 relatively common but mysterious human experiences, 10 rare or questionable human experiences, and, quite possibly, more than 50 other mysterious phenomena.

detail.abstract:
Background

Responsible Artificial Intelligence (Responsible AI) has emerged as a central theme in the global discourse on ethical and trustworthy AI in healthcare. However, there are no universally agreed definition of what constitutes 'responsible AI', the set of underlying principles that should guide development of responsible AI and the approaches used in its assessment. There is also lack of clarity of how principles related to responsible AI are interpreted, operationalised and governed across health systems. This study synthesises global literature on the policy frameworks and legal guardrails used to frame the conceptual foundations and practical application of Responsible AI in healthcare. It proposes a systems-thinking framework that links AI ethics, governance, and adoption of Responsible AI as a new innovation.

Methods

We conducted a systematic review registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251238814). Seven databases were searched for English-language publications from Jan 1, 2010 to Oct 30, 2025 addressing ethics, governance, or policy of AI in healthcare. We extracted and coded principles, governance mechanisms, and implementation tools. Text-mining identified recurring descriptors and conceptual patterns, and mapping of legal guardrails traced how each principle is expressed in statutory and regulatory texts in the EU, USA, and Taiwan. We used a systems-thinking framework that conceptualizes the emergence of Responsible AI from interactions between AI innovation, adoption processes, institutional governance and societal context.

Findings

Of 1,828 records identified, 24 met inclusion criteria. Textual synthesis identified fourteen recurrent Responsible AI principles, of which transparency and explainability were most consistently cited (>90% of publications), followed by fairness and equity, accountability, and safety/robustness (70-90%). Mapping of the guiding legal principles revealed ethical commitments expressed as privacy rights, risk-classification duties, post-market monitoring requirements, and compliance obligations across major legal regimes. However, few publications linked ethical principles to institutional or health-system contexts.

Interpretation

This study consolidates the fragmented landscape of responsible AI in healthcare, identifying common principles and shared meanings, and reframes them within a systems-thinking perspective that integrates innovation, adoption, and regulation. The findings demonstrate that Responsible AI is best understood as a system-level construct rather than a set of isolated ethical rules. Policymakers and health-system leaders are therefore urged to move beyond declarative principles toward adaptive governance frameworks that embed continuous learning, accountability, and equity to ensure AI delivers sustainable public benefit.

detail.abstract: This study investigates how Euroscepticism affected the portfolio choices of Italian retail investors following the Brexit referendum. Using granular investment data, we show that residents of Eurosceptic provinces significantly increased their allocations to UK securities after Brexit (relative to residents of pro-European provinces), suggesting that Eurosceptic investors perceived Brexit as a positive event for UK prospects. Robustness checks show that the results are not driven by potential demographic, geographic, or economic confounders, nor by banks’ advice or broader geographic portfolio rebalancing. Our findings highlight how polarization in political beliefs, when coupled with pivotal geopolitical events, can influence international investment decisions.

title: Signaling Processing Monetary Policy Surprises -Policy, Information, and News in High-Frequency Data

detail.title: Signaling Processing Monetary Policy Surprises -Policy, Information, and News in High-Frequency Data
detail.abstract: High-frequency identification has become the standard approach for identifying monetary policy shocks. Recently, however, this method has come under scrutiny, as several studies show that high-frequency instruments are contaminated by central bank information effects or by the Fed's-responds-to-news channel. Our paper develops a data-driven approach to address both sources of contamination simultaneously. First, we show that instruments from the literature that are orthogonalized to one form of contamination remain vulnerable to the other. Second, we implement a forward regression algorithm to estimate the optimal set of predictors for purifying measures of monetary policy shocks. The algorithm consistently chooses a mix of economic news and central bank information variables. While this confirms that both channels are present in high-frequency monetary policy data, additional analysis reveals that the Fed'sresponds-to-news channel is considerably more robust. Third, using the selected predictors, we estimate distinct shock series for monetary policy, central bank information effects, and the Fed-responds-to-news channel, and study their effects in structural vector autoregression models. We find that monetary policy shocks reduce output and prices while tightening financial conditions. Fed-responds-to-news shocks, by contrast, raise output and prices and ease financial conditions. Finally, central bank information shocks increase output and prices, despite rising interest rates and excess bond premia.

title: Public health impact, cost-effectiveness, and budget impact of HPV vaccination in Kazakhstan: stakeholder engagement and modelling study

detail.title: Public health impact, cost-effectiveness, and budget impact of HPV vaccination in Kazakhstan: stakeholder engagement and modelling study
detail.abstract: Background Cervical cancer kills 900 women in Kazakhstan annually, despite being preventable by human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination. The highly oncogenic types, HPV-16 and HPV-18, are targeted by the quadrivalent HPV vaccine, which was introduced through a two-dose schedule into Kazakhstan’s national immunisation programme in September 2024. We conducted a stakeholder engagement and modelling study to estimate the health impact, cost-effectiveness, and budget impact of HPV vaccination in Kazakhstan and assessed the value of switching to a one-dose schedule. Methods We formed a stakeholder working group of 19 members to collate Kazakhstan-specific data on cervical cancer burden and treatment costs and streamlined 16 ‘what-if’ vaccination scenarios. We used UNIVAC, a static cohort model, to estimate the health impact and cost-effectiveness of vaccinating 10 cohorts of 11-year-old girls (2025-2034) for two-dose and one-dose schedules compared to the counterfactual scenario of no vaccination from the government perspective. Findings Without vaccination, we estimated 22,142 cases and 6,770 deaths from cervical cancer across the life course of the cohorts targeted for vaccination. For every 10% increase in vaccine coverage, we estimated an 8% reduction in cervical cancer burden across the lifetime of the vaccinated women. The one-dose schedule was cost-effective in every model iteration (100%), compared to 82% for the two-dose schedule, at a willingness-to-pay threshold of US$7,700 based on health opportunity cost. Interpretation The two-dose HPV vaccination programme in Kazakhstan is cost-effective. The budget impact of vaccination costs for the one-dose schedule, which is logistically easier to administer and scale up, is half of that of the two-dose schedule with similar health benefits.

title: Unravelling the Persistence of Money Laundering in UK Banks despite Regulatory Reforms: A Critical Evaluation of Key UK Anti-Money Laundering Obligations, Bank Compliance Practices, and the Potential Role of Artificial Intelligence in Shaping Compliance within a Rapidly Evolving Technological Landscape

detail.abstract: Despite successive reforms in the United Kingdom’s anti-money laundering (AML) framework, the persistence of money laundering continues to undermine the integrity of the country’s banking system. To understand this enduring issue, this paper critically evaluates the effectiveness of three core statutory obligations: Customer Due Diligence (CDD) (Regulation 28, MLR 2017), ongoing monitoring (Regulation 28(11)), and the duty to report suspicious transactions (Section 330, Proceeds of Crime Act 2002), against the benchmarks of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF). Additionally, it draws on case studies of Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) enforcement actions to evaluate the FCA’s enforcement strategy and how banks operationalise AML obligations in practice. The analysis demonstrates that the persistence of money laundering is not primarily a result of legislative gaps but rather of weaknesses in enforcement, entrenched profit-driven cultures within banks, and significant operational limitations. The study finds that while FCA sanctions are substantial, they are predominantly reactive and centred on corporate fines, which prove ineffective in driving substantive reform within the sector. Furthermore, within banks, compliance is often treated as a procedural obligation rather than a strategic priority, with outdated systems and fragmented data further constraining its effectiveness. The analysis further explores how banks are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence (AI) to overcome AML compliance challenges at the institutional level. However, while AI offers potential for greater efficiency and improved detection, its deployment also raises significant concerns regarding transparency, bias, data protection, and inaccuracies. Moreover, the current UK AML regime has struggled to keep pace with these technological developments, leaving unresolved questions of oversight and accountability, particularly in the event of errors produced by AI-driven AML compliance systems. By critically examining these issues, this study contributes to legal scholarship and policy by demonstrating that effective reform requires proactive regulatory supervision, greater individual accountability, cultural change within banks, and the development of AIspecific regulatory standards. Ultimately, it advocates for an AML regime that is both attuned to institutional realities and responsive to technological transformation.

detail.abstract: Despite their advantages, multinational enterprises (MNEs) receive significant criticism, particularly with regard to offshoring jobs and shifting profits abroad to avoid taxation. Using administrative data for the universe of Norwegian and French firms and workers, we link these two issues by documenting a negative relation between MNE investment in a tax haven and employment in the high-tax country. In particular, exploiting the 2006 European Court of Justice (ECJ) decision on the Cadbury-Schweppes case which upheld the use of EU tax havens, we are able to establish a causal link in which tax haven use lowers domestic employment by 6%. Heterogeneity analyses reveal that the effects are mainly concentrated among high-skilled workers. We further link the employment changes to the substance requirements mandated by the ECJ's ruling and the secrecy inherent to tax havens.

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the scope and coverage of the Common Reporting Standard (CRS), an international automatic exchange of information regime intended to eliminate bank secrecy and reduce cross-border tax evasion. We obtain new, aggregated CRS data from 26 countries, covering roughly 30% of the global amount reported by the OECD for the year 2022. We first show that cross-border financial wealth continues to be concentrated in tax havens. We then combine our aggregate CRS data with recent estimates of offshore financial wealth to estimate the coverage of the CRS. Our results suggest a coverage rate ranging from 38 to 93% for the subsample of countries we have the most granular data from, highlighting scope for improvement. However, we also show that the volume of data exchanged internationally has increased and improved in quality substantially over recent years, giving reason for longer-term optimism.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the structural crisis of China's real estate and financial systems in 2026, analyzing the mechanisms of equilibrium shift and balance sheet adjustment under incomplete contracts. By integrating an empirical analysis of the "managed liquidation" process with rigorous game-theoretic models based on Tirole (2006), we elucidate how micro-level incentive distortions propagate to macro-level financial instability. The study consists of three parts. Part I provides a comprehensive overview of the structural oversupply in the real estate market, the collapse of the "Land Standard" business model of Local Government Financing Vehicles (LGFVs), and the resulting impairment of the banking sector. We identify that the current state is characterized by "financial repression," where market pricing mechanisms are suspended to defer systemic collapse. Part II constructs a theoretical model linking the Soft Budget Constraint (SBC) to Aggregate Liquidity Shortages. We prove that LGFVs have a rational incentive to strategically deteriorate asset quality ("Shirk") to satisfy the ex-post bailout condition (L ≤ ρ 1-ρ), effectively enforcing a "Too Messy to Fail" status. This anticipation leads to zero ex-ante liquidity hoarding by the private sector, resulting in a systemic liquidity shortage during crises. Consequently, the central government faces a time-inconsistency problem where it is compelled to execute fiscal injections (via Special Sovereign Bonds or PSL) despite ex-ante commitments, establishing a regime of Fiscal Dominance. Part III analyzes the "Baojiaolou" (Guaranteed Delivery of Homes) policy using a Multistage Investment Model with intermediate information acquisition. We demonstrate that the inclusion of social stability costs (S) lowers the optimal project stopping threshold from the economically rational level (τ * F B) to a politically motivated level (τ * Gov). This divergence causes the "excessive continuation" of negative-NPV projects. Furthermore, we show that the "Whitelist" system, intended for screening, transforms into an institutional device to justify fiscal transfers to zombie projects, inducing ex-ante overinvestment and moral hazard among developers.

detail.abstract: This study aims to explore the European Union's (EU) development of polarity characteristics, focusing on how it can establish itself as a distinct geopolitical actor in the evolving multipolar international landscape. The research employs a qualitative comparative analysis of the EU's existing capabilities in economic, military, and regulatory domains, alongside case studies of other major powers. It integrates theoretical frameworks from international relations, including structural realism and liberal institutionalism, to assess the EU's potential for influence and power projection. The findings indicate that the EU possesses significant economic strength and regulatory authority but lacks a cohesive military strategy and demographic vitality necessary for a fully realized geopolitical role. The study highlights the importance of integrating soft and hard power, fostering a unified defense framework, and enhancing demographic policies to support long-term strategic goals. The EU's path to becoming a credible geopolitical pole hinges on its ability to consolidate its diverse capabilities into a coherent strategy. By addressing fragmentation in policy and enhancing its global narrative, the EU can effectively navigate the complexities of multipolarity and assert its influence in international affairs.

title: Ambient Intelligence in Healthcare: Investment Returns and Business Models of CSI-Based Monitoring

detail.title: Ambient Intelligence in Healthcare: Investment Returns and Business Models of CSI-Based Monitoring
detail.abstract: Ambient intelligence in healthcare promises continuous, unobtrusive monitoring of patients and seniors using pervasive sensing embedded in the built environment.[1] WiFi Channel State Information (CSI) sensing has emerged as a particularly attractive modality, offering device-free, contactless and privacy-preserving monitoring of motion, activity and certain vital-sign proxies by leveraging existing WiFi infrastructure.[6, 5] This paper analyzes investment returns and business models for CSI-based ambient intelligence in healthcare, focusing on hospitals, elderly care facilities and home-health platforms. We develop cost-benefit and discounted cash flow (DCF) models for CSI deployments, compare them with camera-and wearable-centric alternatives, and discuss risk-sharing arrangements between technology vendors, providers and payers.[7] Using stylized scenarios, we show that CSI-based ambient monitoring can achieve positive net present value (NPV) within 2-4 years at scale, particularly when coupled with outcome-based reimbursement and platform business models.

title: WiFi as Infrastructure: Valuation Impact of CSI Sensing on Smart Buildings and REIT Portfolios

detail.title: WiFi as Infrastructure: Valuation Impact of CSI Sensing on Smart Buildings and REIT Portfolios
detail.abstract: WiFi Channel State Information (CSI) sensing is emerging as a practical way to transform existing WiFi networks into dense, non-intrusive sensor grids that can provide occupancy, activity and environmental information without deploying large numbers of dedicated sensors or cameras.[1, 2] This paper interprets CSI sensing as an infrastructure layer for smart buildings and examines how it can affect net operating income (NOI), risk, and valuation of Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT) portfolios. We first summarize key CSI sensing capabilities and their technical underpinnings, including occupancy detection, people counting and respiration monitoring using commodity WiFi hardware.[1, 3, 4] We then connect these capabilities to documented smart-building value drivers such as energy savings, improved tenant experience and ESG-linked cap rate compression.[14, 16, 17, 18] Using a stylized discounted cash flow (DCF) framework, we show that CSI-enabled smart building programmes can plausibly generate per-asset value uplifts in the 8-15% range, and several percentage points of uplift at the REIT portfolio level when adoption is scaled, under assumptions consistent with published energy and smart-building case studies.[19, 20]

title: Greenhouse Gas Emissions of US States: Decoupling, Outsourcing, and Overshoot
affiliations: MODUL University Vienna, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Independent Researcher, Universität für Bodenkultur Wien (BOKU) and Norwegian University of Life Sciences

detail.title: Greenhouse Gas Emissions of US States: Decoupling, Outsourcing, and Overshoot

publicationDetails.detailsText: ECOLEC-D-26-00349

detail.abstract: Achieving global climate targets requires rapid and sustained reductions in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, yet progress remains uneven across scales and overall emissions continue to rise. While the United States (US) is a leading emitter, much of its mitigation policy occurs at the subnational level. This study provides the first comprehensive state-level compilation and analysis of territorial (TE) and consumption-based GHG emissions (CBE) across all 50 US states from 2012 to 2019. By combining these indicators with GDP and internationally recognized per-capita emission targets we assess the extent of decoupling, outsourcing, and ecological overshoot among states.Our findings reveal persistent discrepancies between CBE and TE, indicating substantial outsourcing of environmental impacts from wealthier, service-oriented states to those with resource-intensive economies and to foreign producers. While 24% of states achieved statistically significant rates of absolute decoupling of GDP from both CBE and TE during the study period, none of the 50 states are projected to meet the 2 tonnes GHG per-capita threshold consistent with limiting warming to 1.5–2 °C before 2100.Many states that appear to perform well from a territorial perspective continue to outsource a substantial share of their GHG footprint to other states and countries, highlighting persistent patterns of environmental cost-shifting both within the national economy and internationally. Meanwhile, states with the highest emissions per capita are fossil fuel exporters and their CBE emissions are generally far lower than their TE emissions, indicating emissions in these states are driven in part by consumption in other regions.

title: Beyond Cameras: The Economics of Privacy-Preserving Security Systems Using WiFi CSI
affiliations: XZENT SOLUTIONS PRIVATE LIMITED

detail.title: Beyond Cameras: The Economics of Privacy-Preserving Security Systems Using WiFi CSI
detail.abstract: Traditional security systems rely heavily on camera-based surveillance, which raises recurring concerns about privacy, data governance and regulatory risk in buildings and public spaces.[1, 2] WiFi Channel State Information (CSI) sensing offers an alternative by using existing WiFi infrastructure as a passive motion and activity detector, enabling intrusion detection, anomaly detection and occupant monitoring without capturing identifiable images.[1, 3, 4] This paper analyzes the economics of privacy-preserving security systems that use WiFi CSI as a primary sensing modality, focusing on capital expenditure (capex), operating expenditure (opex), false-alarm costs and regulatory risk relative to camera-centric systems.[5, 6] We examine threat vectors specific to CSIbased systems, model the cost of privacy-preserving defenses, and evaluate deployment scenarios in elderly care, office and logistics settings. Using stylized cost-benefit and discounted cash flow (DCF) models, we show that WiFi CSI-based systems can reduce lifecycle security costs while improving privacy posture, especially in environments where WiFi coverage already exists and where regulatory or reputational exposure to visual surveillance is high. We further show how sensor fusion (WiFi CSI plus selective cameras) can optimize total cost of ownership for diverse asset types within a REIT portfolio.[1, 9, 4]

detail.abstract: For centuries, scholars within the just war tradition have sought to develop objective criteria for entering into conflict (jus ad bellum) and for just conduct in war (jus in bello). Though JWT scholars have increasingly recognized institutional challenges and proposed various reforms, these analyses lack a systematic examination of the underlying incentive structures that shape institutional performance. This paper fills this gap by analyzing JWT in constitutional democracies through the lens of public choice economics. We show how specific mechanisms-information asymmetries, principal-agent problems, rational ignorance, bureaucratic incentives, and special interests-systematically undermine JWT compliance. By revealing the micro-foundations of JWT implementation in constitutional democracies, we contribute to ongoing debates about feasible institutional designs for just war principles.

detail.abstract: Public support is key for implementing urgently needed socio-ecological transitions, including climate policies. To achieve such transitions, post-growth concepts as alternatives to growth-based models have seen increasing support among academics and activists. However, important gaps remain. In the first place, less is known about citizens’ support for post-growth. In parallel, evidence is needed on whether public support for climate policies can increase by linking them to a broader socio-economic transition following post-growth approaches. Using nationally representative survey data collected from German citizens, first, we find that the post-growth concept does not achieve majority support. However, we shed light on an important but under-explored dimension of post-growth: the aspect of global fairness and responsibility. We find that it is particularly this component of post-growth that people support. Second, by linking post-growth to specific climate policy instruments (the energy transition including the coal exit) currently implemented in Germany, we find that those people in support of post-growth also exhibit higher support for the energy transition. In addition, a key result of this study is the potential of increasing overall public support for climate policies by implementing it within a post-growth framework, i.e. combining it with more structural socio-economic policy instruments. We investigate in particular the crucial role of fears for policy support.

detail.title: Land-use optimization to support landscape transformation policies aimed at reducing the probability of an extreme fire regime at the lowest possible cost

publicationDetails.detailsText: ECOLEC-D-26-00493

detail.abstract: This study develops an analytical framework integrating a fire regime model and a land-use choice model to maximize the net economic returns from land use while keeping the probability of an extreme fire regime (EFR) below a socially acceptable level, or wildfire policy constraint. This analytical framework is applied and tested at a nationwide scale, for the whole of mainland Portugal, where an EFR characterized by high cumulative burnt areas and their temporal concentration has been expanding, and a Landscape Transformation Programme has been adopted by Government. By taking into account biophysical and socioeconomic heterogeneity, and thus variation in the relative profitability of different land-use classes across the country, the optimization model yields case-specific land-use solutions that respect the wildfire policy constraint on EFR probability at a minimum cost for each particular landscape area. By running the model for successively lower levels of the EFR probability, we got the required areal extent, intensity, direction (in terms of land-use change) and marginal cost of landscape transformation for each level of policy ambition about the EFR probability reduction. This marginal cost rises with the level of policy ambition, which raises issues about the affordability and optimality of each level of policy ambition. The approach is assessed as useful to promote the cost-effectiveness of the Landscape Transformation Programme in Portugal as well as that of policies in different countries with similar policy goals and fire regimes.

title: Integrating revealed and stated preferences to value recreational fishing and seagrass restoration in South Australia
affiliations: Flinders University, University of Adelaide, Flinders University and University of Tasmania - Tasmanian School of Business & Economics

detail.title: Integrating revealed and stated preferences to value recreational fishing and seagrass restoration in South Australia

publicationDetails.detailsText: ECOLEC-D-26-00383

detail.abstract: Coastal and marine habitat degradation threatens recreational fisheries and associated ecosystem services in South Australia, particularly through the loss of seagrass meadows that underpin regional biodiversity and angler activity. This study quantifies realised and potential recreational value by integrating revealed and stated preference methods to triangulate welfare estimates. Drawing on recent statewide survey data, the analysis examines 1,260 recreational fishers who together undertake about 34,000 fishing days annually. A zero-inflated negative binomial travel cost model with regional fixed-effects estimates baseline consumer surplus, capturing excess zeros and unobserved site heterogeneity. Results indicate substantial recreational use value, with an average annual consumer surplus of AUD3,450 per angler and an implied per-trip surplus of approximately $130, corresponding to statewide benefits approaching $1 billion per year. A contingent valuation model reveals significant spatially heterogeneous willingness to pay ~$35 for higher trip costs and $120 for a one-off restoration contribution. These values represent a plausible fraction of the per-trip surplus. These findings deliver spatially explicit policy-relevant welfare measures to guide marine habitat restoration, recreational fisheries management, and investment in blue carbon strategies.

title: How Do Value Added Taxes Affect Wages and Labor?
affiliations: Free University of Berlin (FUB) and Freie Universität, Berlin

detail.title: How Do Value Added Taxes Affect Wages and Labor?
detail.abstract: We analyze how value added taxes (VATs) affect labor market outcomes (firms' employee costs, wages, hours worked, employment). While VATs are designed to tax consumption, they are levied at the firm level, which creates potential spillovers to labor markets. We hypothesize that VATs affect wages and employment through two channels: an inflation adjustment effect, where employees demand higher wages to compensate for VAT-induced price increases; and a profitability effect, where incomplete pass-through reduces firms' net sales and profits, putting downward pressure on wages and employment. We exploit variation in VAT rates, measuring labor market outcomes at the firm and country level. We find economically significant negative effects of VAT rates at the firm level on employee costs and at the country level on wages and employment. At the firm level, a one percentage point increase in the standard VAT rate corresponds to a 3.886% reduction in employee costs. At the country level, the same increase is associated with a 2.802% decline in average nominal wages. We find a 1.444% decline in employment at the country level following a one percentage point increase in the VAT rate. For working hours, the evidence is inconclusive and at most suggests a reduction. Heterogeneity analyses suggest that small firms and firms with high profit margins react stronger; among the employees, the age group 15-24 years is hit hardest. Our study provides the first systematic cross-country evidence on the labor market consequences of VATs.

detail.abstract: Over the past few decades, there has been a shift of people from using traditional payment methods to digital methods, thus creating innovation in the payment system. Nowadays, the market is determined to bring a different culture to Albania. The purpose of this study, which is based on the use of credit cards in the Albanian market, especially in Tirana, is to determine the attitude of society towards these credit cards. A questionnaire distributed among 100 consumers was used for primary data collection. This study contains both qualitative analysis and quantitative data analysis. The qualitative analysis addresses the ABC model of behavior, the use of credit cards, and the inflation problems caused by their use. The quantitative analysis highlights model statistics as well as the study of econometric analysis, based on the independent variables that are considered, such as monthly income level, security, prestige, and interest rate, which are thought to have a strong relationship with the use of credit cards as well as the expenses incurred during their use. Age, gender, monthly income, employment status, the reason for use, frequency of use per month, and duration of use are considered in the statistical model. Various tests have been developed to provide an accurate estimate of the relationship of variables using the SPSS Statistics program. All independent variables have exhibited a positive impact concerning the dependent variable. This paper aims to show the perceptions of people who use credit cards and those who hold a negative attitude about their use.

detail.abstract:
Robert D. Atkinson is the founder and president of the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, a prominent K-Street think tank. Dr. Atkinson is a longtime KIET collaborator and friend of the institution. This article is part of a series of works by influential scholars being published by KIET as part of its 50th Anniversary Global Perspectives Series.  

The global techno-economic environment has changed in fundamental ways that require a similar change in South Korea's overarching strategy and implementation of technoeconomic growth and competitiveness policies. In particular, Korean policy will need to find new ways to address the challenges from the United States (protectionism) and China (techno-economic aggression), while at the same time committing to moving from fast follower to global innovation leader, and driving productivity growth throughout all sectors of the economy, especially outside of manufacturing. The political will for Korea to succeed in the previous international order, which persisted from the late 1960s to the mid-2000s, was generally supportive. It's not clear whether that will to make the institutionally challenging changes needed to survive, if not thrive, in the next era exists today. But the first step to creating that drive is to articulate the challenges of today and the need for a new strategic approach. This article modestly and tentatively lays out four key challenges and some suggested approaches for addressing them.
