title: Impact of Widespread Heat Pump Adoption on Grid Reinforcement and Network Tariff Equity
affiliations: and Technische Universität München (TUM) - TUM School of Management

detail.title: Impact of Widespread Heat Pump Adoption on Grid Reinforcement and Network Tariff Equity

publicationDetails.detailsText: ENEECO-D-26-00391

detail.abstract: The increasing adoption of residential heat pumps significantly strains electricity distribution infrastructure, necessitating substantial grid investments. We use representative European grid models to analyze the impact of heat pump-induced grid investments on electricity tariffs and uncover equity issues in volumetric tariff systems – a predominant tariff design in many Continental European countries. Current tariff practices disproportionately allocate reinforcement costs to non-heat-pump households, who cross-finance up to 85% of these costs at lower adoption levels. Consequently, households may face tariff increases of >20%, which would significantly exceed historical electricity price growth. We recommend implementing policies incentivizing more cost-reflective network planning. In addition, alternative tariff structures warrant further investigation for their potential to defer reinforcement costs and mitigate emerging distributional inequalities. These measures support equitable cost recovery, grid stability, and sustainable electrification of residential heating.

title: Information Design in Supply Chains with Priority Suppliers
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, ESMT European School of Management and Technology and

detail.title: Information Design in Supply Chains with Priority Suppliers
detail.abstract: Problem definition: This paper studies the information design problem of a retailer facing two upstream suppliers to whom it can privately disclose information about market demand. One supplier holds priority in fulfilling orders, while the other serves as a backup. The retailer seeks to minimize expected lost-sales costs, whereas suppliers minimize the sum of lost-sales and excess-inventory holding costs. Methodology/results: We model the interaction between the retailer and suppliers using a Bayesian persuasion framework in which the retailer commits ex ante to an information disclosure policy and privately sends demand signals to each supplier, who then choose production quantities. Our main finding is that asymmetric disclosure characterizes the retailer's optimal policy. Specifically, the retailer strategically favors the lower-priority supplier by providing more informative signals, while keeping the higher-priority supplier relatively less informed. This result relies on very mild assumptions on demand and remains robust to heterogeneous critical ratios and alternative procurement rules. Managerial implications: Our results highlight that the value of information sharing depends critically on how disclosure policies interact with procurement structures. In priority sourcing environments, selectively informing lower-priority suppliers can be more effective than uniformly sharing information across suppliers in reducing the retailer's expected shortage costs.

title: Incentives and Creativity in Groups—Experimental Evidence on Creative Processes and Dimensions
affiliations: Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz - Gutenberg School of Management and Economics

detail.title: Incentives and Creativity in Groups—Experimental Evidence on Creative Processes and Dimensions
detail.abstract: Creativity and teamwork are essential in today's rapidly evolving labor market, yet little is known about how incentives shape creative group processes across multiple creativity dimensions, specifically quantity, quality, and originality. I introduce a novel verbal creative coordination task to incentivize and objectively measure these dimensions of creativity and to generate insights into the full creative group process. Thereby, this paper investigates how idea generation, evaluation, and selection can be effectively incentivized in groups and which incentive scheme maximizes innovation-ideas that are both high in quality and originality. In a laboratory experiment with 640 participants, groups are randomly assigned to a control or one of three group-level relative performance pay treatments targeting either quantity, quality, or originality. Results show that quantity incentives lead to broader exploration, increasing both the number and average originality of ideas, and outperform all other treatments on the combined indicator of innovative ideas. Quality incentives improve idea quality, while originality incentives fail to boost originality. Incentives mainly operate through higher individual effort rather than group dynamics. Across all conditions, the evaluation and selection phases act as a bottleneck, with highly original ideas systematically discarded. These findings highlight that maximizing creative output requires incentives that promote exploration and structures that preserve original ideas.

title: Qualitative Meta-Analysis with System Dynamics Modeling for Process Theory Development
affiliations: Tilburg University - Tilburg University School of Economics and Management and Mays Business School, Texas A&M University

detail.title: Qualitative Meta-Analysis with System Dynamics Modeling for Process Theory Development

publicationDetails.detailsText: System Dynamics Review (forthcoming)

detail.abstract: Management research has been dominated by variance theories that explain outcomes through statistical associations. While process theory complements variance theory by focusing on how and why events, activities, and choices interact over time, it remains challenging to acquire rich, longitudinal process data and translate them into novel, abstract process theories. We propose integrating qualitative meta-analysis (QMA) with system dynamics (SD) modeling to address these challenges. QMA systematically synthesizes temporally rich evidence across multiple qualitative case studies, while SD provides a formal language for articulating causal mechanisms, accommodating temporal complexity, and testing dynamic hypotheses. Using a recent application to servitization, we illustrate how QMA-SD can be implemented in a step-by-step manner. Beyond its substantive contribution to the servitization literature, we demonstrate the broader potential of QMA-SD for generating empirically grounded, generalizable, and testable process theories.

title: Do U.S. Sanctions Significantly Impact the Financing Constraints of Chinese-listed Firms?
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics, Shenzhen University, Department of Accounting and Corporate Governance and

detail.title: Do U.S. Sanctions Significantly Impact the Financing Constraints of Chinese-listed Firms?
detail.abstract: This study examines whether U.S. sanctions significantly impact the financing constraints of Chinese listed firms. Using a uniquely constructed dataset of Chinese A-share firms spanning the 2007 to 2021 period that were directly impacted by the U.S. sanctions, we provide strong evidence showing a positive relationship between sanctions and financing constraints. Additional analyses indicate that the positive relationship between sanctions and financing constraints is more (less) pronounced for firms with greater risk exposure (strong market position, strong innovation and research capabilities, and effective government support policies). Sanctions also increase the financing costs for affected firms, shorten their financing duration, and complicate their access to financing. Finally, various endogeneity tests and robustness checks confirm our baseline results. Overall, our study provides important insights into the detrimental effect of U.S. sanctions on Chinese firms' financing constraints.

title: Patterns and Inequality in Household Education Expenditure in India
affiliations: RTM Nagpur University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Patterns and Inequality in Household Education Expenditure in India
detail.abstract: This study investigates the patters and determinants of household expenditure in India, utilizing a novel livelihood-based analytical framework. Drawing on unit-level data from the NSS 80th Round (2025) Comprehensive Modular Survey: Education 2025 encompassing 57,742 enrolled students, the research moves beyond traditional urban-rural or income-level binaries to examine how economic stability and occupational types influence educational investment. The findings reveal a significant hierarchical gradient in spending. The findings reveal a significant hierarchical gradient in spending, with urban households with regular wage employment spend 5.6 times more per student annually, contrasting sharply with rural casual agricultural laborers. The study employs the Concentration Index (CI), yielding a value of 0.36, indicating substantial pro-rich inequality, suggesting that educational resources are disproportionately concentrated among wealthier households and that family income remains a primary determinant of educational opportunity. The study concludes that education financing policies must shift toward livelihood-specific interventions to mitigate deep-seated economic disparities and foster equitable access to quality education in India.

title: The Cultural Distance Spectrum (CDS): A Framework for Measuring Identity Adaptation in Human Mobility

detail.title: The Cultural Distance Spectrum (CDS): A Framework for Measuring Identity Adaptation in Human Mobility

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal, financial, or institutional conflicts of interest related to this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study, as it is a conceptual and theoretical framework and did not involve human participants, personal data, or experimental procedures.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Global human mobility has expanded rapidly across tourism, education, labour, and long-term settlement. Advances in transportation, regulatory systems, and institutional coordination have significantly reduced barriers to movement. Yet despite improved access and logistics, dissatisfaction, disengagement, and integration failure remain common across mobility contexts, even where economic incentives, safety conditions, and formal eligibility requirements are met.

Existing assessment models primarily evaluate destinations and institutions through external indicators such as distance, development levels, language proficiency, and safety metrics. While these measures are effective for determining feasibility and risk, they offer limited insight into the lived experience of adaptation after movement occurs. As a result, mobility outcomes are frequently explained retrospectively, without a structured way to anticipate where strain is likely to emerge.

This paper argues that a key missing variable in mobility assessment is identity adaptation. Movement across borders places individuals within unfamiliar systems of communication, social interaction, institutional behaviour, and public norms. The cumulative effort required to adjust across these domains constitutes an adaptation burden that is neither random nor purely subjective, yet remains largely unmanaged.

To address this gap, the paper introduces the Cultural Distance Spectrum (CDS), a framework that conceptualizes cultural distance as the degree of identity adaptation required to function comfortably within a given social and institutional environment. The CDS situates adaptation demand along a continuous 0–100 spectrum, emphasizing relational and directional variation rather than binary cultural classification. Eight cultural impact dimensions are identified to structure how adaptation pressure accumulates, and characteristic experiential zones are mapped across the spectrum.

The paper further demonstrates how sustainable levels of cultural distance vary by mobility purpose and outlines a family of context-specific indices derived from the CDS to support institutional planning. By providing a structured language for anticipating adaptation strain, the Cultural Distance Spectrum offers a foundation for more realistic expectation-setting and more sustainable mobility outcomes.

title:
Triangular Liquidity Frictions
Institutional Legibility, Sovereignty, and the Architecture of Global Settlement

detail.title:
Triangular Liquidity Frictions
Institutional Legibility, Sovereignty, and the Architecture of Global Settlement

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This paper is a working paper and reflects the author’s analysis at the time of writing. Comments and feedback are welcome.

detail.abstract:
Why are some state interventions absorbed smoothly by global markets while others generate persistent friction, spreads, and exclusion—despite comparable scale and intent?

This working paper introduces institutional legibility as a missing explanatory variable in the analysis of global liquidity and monetary power. Existing approaches emphasize volumes, balance sheets, or hierarchy within the dollar system, but struggle to explain why extreme policies in some jurisdictions (e.g. Japan) are treated as stabilizing, while interventions elsewhere (e.g. China) are perceived as destabilizing.

I argue that the decisive factor is not the quantity of liquidity supplied, but whether state intervention is institutionally legible—that is, whether its triggers, constraints, and exit conditions are sufficiently readable for markets and counterparties to model, price, and absorb it.

The paper develops a simple Legibility Test (Trigger–Constraint–Exit) and applies it to a comparative analysis of the United States, Japan, and China. The United States exhibits self-referential legibility as the issuer of the dollar-based settlement system; Japan represents legible extremity, where massive balance-sheet expansion remains compatible with global expectations; China operates through administrative liquidity, which stabilizes domestically but remains externally illegible, generating friction at the global settlement interface.

An extended section introduces India as a distinct interface strategy, demonstrating how non-core states can engineer partial legibility through platform-mediated coordination without monetary dominance.

The analysis is explicitly positioned within the dollar-centered global settlement system and is descriptive rather than normative. It explains how the system currently filters intervention, not how it ought to function, and treats alternative legibility standards as an open empirical question.

The paper contributes to debates on global liquidity, monetary sovereignty, and geopolitical fragmentation, with implications for swap lines, risk premia, and the weaponization of financial infrastructure.

title: Designing Viable Flood Microinsurance for Bangalore Urban Informal Settlements
affiliations: Tyche Investments - Climate Consulting Group

detail.title: Designing Viable Flood Microinsurance for Bangalore Urban Informal Settlements
detail.abstract: Urban informal settlements, highly vulnerable to climate-induced flooding, lack access to viable risk-transfer mechanisms. This study investigates how low-cost insurance can be designed for such contexts, using Bangalore, India, as a case. Employing a novel computational theory-building approach, we synthesize secondary data to develop an integrated System Dynamics and Agent-Based Model. This virtual laboratory simulates interactions between insurance design, household behaviour, and flood shocks in a risk-free environment. We test key design levers: index type, subsidies, distribution channels, and contract simplicity. Our findings reveal that product success is determined less by isolated features and more by interrupting systemic feedback loops of "Asset Erosion" and "Trust Erosion." Global sensitivity analysis identifies trust in institutions and social network strength as more critical for uptake than premium price. The most robust configuration combines a multi-parametric index (reducing basis risk), CBO-led distribution (building trust), and a tiered subsidy (enhancing affordability), supported by a public reinsurance backstop. We conclude that effective design requires a paradigm shift from a productcentric to a system-centric view, creating hybrid products that are technically sound, socially embedded, and financially structured through tripartite partnerships. The study provides a simulation-validated framework for developing context-specific, climate-resilient flood insurance for the urban poor.

title: Selecting the Optimal Number of Futures Contracts for the Next Trade Using C++

detail.title: Selecting the Optimal Number of Futures Contracts for the Next Trade Using C++

keywords: two theorems of Khinchin on St. Petersburg game

detail.abstract: The year 2026 marks the 70th anniversary of the publication of John Larry Kelly Jr.'s paper "A New Interpretation of Information Rate." He noticed a similarity between the transmission rate defined by Claude Shannon and "the exponential rate of growth of  the gambler's capital" and suggested optimizing the latter. The differentiability of functions underlying Shannon and Kelly's formulas does not apply in trading. A whole number of traded futures contracts, margin requirements, and a long chain of losses can destroy an account. The discreteness of prices and money, amplified by high futures leverage and large trading positions, hinders analytical optimization of a constant allocation fraction. To overcome these limitations, discrete equations formulated using iterals for the introduced stochastic growth rates and account values are proposed, as well as Monte Carlo simulations based on empirical profit and loss distribution functions, which are illustrated using two programs written in C++. Distribution functions and their inverses are derived for the Standard C++ class templates of the discrete, and piecewise constant and linear distributions. Interface-Concrete-Handle C++ design pattern combining generic, object-oriented, and meta programming is suggested.

title: Political Intervention, Sovereignty Erosion and Strategic Control of Resources: Evidence from the Venezuelan Case: (2026)

detail.title: Political Intervention, Sovereignty Erosion and Strategic Control of Resources: Evidence from the Venezuelan Case: (2026)
detail.abstract: This article examines how political intervention and the selective use of international legal norms reshape the international business environment, using Venezuela as a critical case. Drawing on insights from international law and international political economy, the study argues that interventions justified through discourses of democracy, stability and governance often conceal strategic economic objectives, particularly the control of natural resources. The paper analyses policy statements, sanctions regimes and intervention practices affecting Venezuela and evaluates their implications for foreign firms, host-state sovereignty and global energy markets. The findings suggest that such interventions generate systemic uncertainty for international business by weakening legal predictability, normalising exceptional measures and altering the balance of bargaining power between states and multinational enterprises. The article contributes to international business scholarship by demonstrating how geopolitical strategies and legal ambiguity function as mechanisms of indirect economic appropriation, with long-term consequences for global governance, investment decisions and the stability of international business system. The Venezuelan case is treated as a critical case given its strategic relevance to global energy markets and its exposure to sustained external political and economic pressure.

detail.abstract: ZARYNX Theory presents a foundational economic framework that defines economies through strict structural boundaries rather than ideology, behavior, or historical context. The theory asserts that economic activity exists only where scarcity, rivalry, and constraint-bound allocation simultaneously occur. By enforcing hard entry conditions, mandatory measurability, and explicit falsifiability criteria, ZARYNX establishes economics as a constraint-science applicable across pre-industrial societies, Modern market economies, Digital platform economies, AI-driven and automated systems. The theory is explanatory rather than prescriptive and is designed to remain valid under technological and civilizational change.

title: Institutional Investment and International Risk-sharing
affiliations: University of Melbourne, Faculty of Business and Economics

detail.title: Institutional Investment and International Risk-sharing
detail.abstract: I develop and estimate an asset-pricing model with global institutional investors and home-biased retail investors. International risk-sharing depends on institutional mandate coverage, risk-bearing capacity, and cross-country return correlation. The market-wide local risk premium decomposes into an institutional local risk premium and a retail local risk premium, governed by the risk-bearing capacity of each investor group. Using individual stock returns and global institutional ownership across 41 economies, I find that both local risk premia are economically important and exhibit distinct cyclical dynamics. Cross-market variation reflects differences in institutional risk-bearing capacity and return correlation, while stock-level ownership shapes factor exposures.

title: Demography and the Current Account: A Case-Study of Italy
affiliations: Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: Demography and the Current Account: A Case-Study of Italy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 969
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the role of demography in driving the current account (CA) ‘norms’ (i.e. the medium-term CA values consistent with economic fundamentals and desired policies) which are estimated by several international institutions. The paper makes two distinct contributions. First, it highlights that the use of population projections sourced from different institutions (namely, the United Nations, Eurostat, and Istat) can significantly alter the size of the positive contribution of demography to CA norms. In particular, for Italy and the other main euro-area economies, CA norm estimates are significantly lower if alternative projections to the more pessimistic UN projections are employed. Second, the paper extends the reference CA model to incorporate labour market indicators, consistently with a life-cycle hypothesis. This improvement results in additional downward revisions to CA norms, especially regarding Italy. Jointly, these findings underscore the importance of exercising great caution when interpreting model-based CA norm estimates for policy evaluation and external imbalance assessments.

title: More on VARs and Local Projections Equivalence: Unit Roots and Multiple Instruments
affiliations: Newcastle Business School, University of Surrey and University of Pavia - Department of Economics and Management

detail.title: More on VARs and Local Projections Equivalence: Unit Roots and Multiple Instruments
detail.abstract: We show that the equivalence in population between impulse responses in Vector Autoregressions (VARs) and Local Projections (LPs) can be extended to (possibly cointegrated) unit roots with unrestricted lag structure. We also prove that structural estimation with multiple instruments for multiple endogenous regressors (LP-IV) is equivalent to a recursively block-identified Structural VAR, where the block of instruments is ordered first. Simulations and two applications illustrate our results.

title: Digital Financial Literacy and Its Influence on Investment Decision-Making by the Millenial Generation
affiliations: Bung Karno University

detail.title: Digital Financial Literacy and Its Influence on Investment Decision-Making by the Millenial Generation

publicationDetails.detailsText: SSRN Working Paper Series, Faculty of Economics and Business, Bung Karno University, 2026.

detail.abstract: The expansion of digital technology has significantly reshaped the financial environment, particularly in how people obtain financial information and determine investment choices. This transformation highlights the growing importance of digital financial literacy, especially for the millennial generation, which is closely connected to digital platforms and financial technology. This paper seeks to reinterpret the concept of digital financial literacy and analyze its role in influencing investment decision-making among millennials. Employing a qualitative descriptive method through a comprehensive literature review, this study examines relevant theories and previous empirical studies related to digital financial literacy, millennial investment behavior, and decision-making processes in the digital era. The analysis indicates that digital financial literacy is a key factor in encouraging more rational, informed, and systematic investment decisions. Millennials with higher digital financial literacy levels are generally more capable of understanding investment risks, critically assessing digital financial information, and aligning investment decisions with long-term financial objectives. In contrast, inadequate digital financial literacy often leads to impulsive and speculative investment behavior, frequently driven by social media trends and external influences. Overall, the findings emphasize that digital financial literacy goes beyond mere technological access, encompassing analytical skills and responsible use of digital financial services. Strengthening digital financial literacy is therefore essential to enhance investment decision quality and support the long-term financial stability of the millennial generation.

title: Timely Quarterly Indicators of Household Consumption and Disposable Income for the Italian Regions

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 970
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This study introduces an innovative econometric methodology for developing timely quarterly indicators of household income and consumption for all Italian regions and autonomous provinces. Leveraging a comprehensive statistical database spanning from 1995 to 2022, the methodology utilizes basic indicators from the real economy and monetary sectors. These indicators are condensed into regional common factors and combined with national aggregates to model the annual regional time series published by Istat. Two selection approaches, Stepwise Forward Selection (SFS) and sparse Temporal Disaggregation (spTD) using LASSO-type methods identify relevant local factors. These models interpolate observed annual figures ex-post and provide ex-ante estimates of quarterly regional aggregates with a 90-day post-quarter-end lag. In-sample evaluations show high model fit, particularly with the spTD methodology. Out-of-sample forecasting confirms satisfactory predictive performance, albeit with varying precision across regions. Overall, this methodology yields reliable indicators of regional household income and consumption dynamics, offering timely insights that are crucial for short-term economic analysis and answer the challenges posed by official statistics in Italy, which are annual and released with a one-year lag.

title: Life-Cycle Health Effects of Compulsory Military Service in the GDR
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Life-Cycle Health Effects of Compulsory Military Service in the GDR
detail.abstract: We examine the long-term health effects of peacetime conscription in the German Democratic Republic using a regression-discontinuity design that exploits the introduction of conscription in 1962 and resulting variation in conscription between birth cohorts. Conscription eligibility increases musculoskeletal hospitalizations later in life, consistent with descriptive evidence on overuse injuries during service, and raises sick leave during draft-eligible ages and after the German reunification. These effects are not explained by education or wages but partly by occupational sorting into physically demanding jobs. Our findings highlight lasting health burdens of military service and long-term consequences of physical strain and injury.

title: Financial Stability Considerations on bail-In
affiliations: Bank of Italy

detail.title: Financial Stability Considerations on bail-In

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 968
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper provides an economic analysis of the challenges to the bail-in regime in terms of its ability to affect the structure of incentives within large banks and to solve the problem posed by intermediaries that are classed as ‘too big to fail’ (TBTF). It first explains the peculiar role of large banks in the modern financial system and the impact of their failures on financial stability – both of which aspects are invoked to justify their differential treatment in a crisis. This discussion of the rationale for a bail-in regime helps understand the economic basis and the minimum conditions for the tool to be applied efficiently. The paper shows that European bail-in regulations involve complex rules and mechanisms that can be accompanied by discretionary aspects, potentially leading to uncertainties in the application of the procedure and difficulties in in achieving its objectives. A credible regulatory framework and clear decision-making processes would strengthen market discipline and reduce moral hazard. Finally, the paper argues that the bail-in procedure seems to be less viable, from a functional perspective, in the instance of a banking crisis with potentially systemic implications.

title: Decentralising Environmental Public Spending: From Political Platforms to Actual Policies in the EU Countries
affiliations: Università degli Studi di Roma Tre, University of Urbino and University of Urbino Carlo Bo

detail.title: Decentralising Environmental Public Spending: From Political Platforms to Actual Policies in the EU Countries

publicationDetails.detailsText: FEEM Working Paper No. 07-2026
publicationDetails.journalName: FEEM Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Environmental challenges increasingly shape political discourses across Europe, yet their influence on actual environmental governance remains unclear. This paper examines the political economy mechanisms linking environmental change, party platforms, and the decentralisation of environmental protection expenditure in 27 EU member states from 2002 to 2022. We distinguish between political signalling-the commitments parties make in electoral manifestos-and policy implementation, measured through actual decentralised environmental spending. Our results reveal a sharp asymmetry: while extreme events substantially increase the salience of environmental protection in party platforms, they do not translate into changes in the territorial allocation of environmental expenditure. Instead, decentralisation responds primarily to long-term structural conditions, such as the relative weight of locally versus globally relevant emissions. Political orientations of governing coalitions, whether on environmental issues or decentralisation, show no systematic association with spending outcomes. Taken together, these findings highlight a persistent gap between electoral incentives and policy implementation in multilevel environmental governance, consistent with public-choice theories emphasising institutional inertia and limited political responsiveness beyond the stage of platform competition.

title: Fiscal Drag in Greece
affiliations: Bank of Greece and Bank of Greece - Economic Research Department

detail.title: Fiscal Drag in Greece

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Greece Economic Bulletin, Issue No. 62
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Greece Economic Bulletin

detail.abstract: This paper uses a microsimulation approach to analyse the phenomenon of "fiscal drag" in Greece, i.e. the increase in tax revenues that arises when nominal tax bases grow, while the parameters of the personal income tax (PIT) system remain unchanged in nominal terms. First, we estimate the phenomenon in terms of the tax-to-base elasticity, which captures the responsiveness of PIT revenue to changes in the tax base under an unchanged legislation. The results suggest an elasticity of almost 1.8 in 2019, implying a built-in progressivity in the PIT system and, therefore, potential for fiscal drag. We further decompose this elasticity to identify its main drivers across income sources (labour, capital, self-employment, pensions and benefits) and tax parameters (tax brackets, tax deductions/credits) as well as across the income distribution. Second, we assess fiscal drag in practice between 2019 and 2023 by comparing actual PIT revenues (incorporating observed income growth and legislative changes) against counterfactual 2023 scenarios simulating alternative indexation practices. We quantify the actual impact of fiscal drag, defined as a share of GDP, and the extent to which government policies have managed to offset it. The findings indicate that, although Greece has no formal indexation of tax parameters, the tax policy reforms implemented between 2019 and 2023 more than offset the potential effects of fiscal drag, keeping PIT revenues broadly stable as a share of GDP, while slightly reducing the average effective tax rate. Overall, the results highlight that, during a period of rapid nominal income growth, Greece's PIT reforms improved both the progressivity and the redistributive capacity of the tax system, while safeguarding PIT revenue. These insights are relevant for the design of future tax policy interventions.

title: Incorporating Micro Data into Macro Models Using Pseudo VARs

detail.abstract: This paper develops a method to incorporate micro data, available as repeated crosssections, into macro VAR models to understand the distributional effects of macroeconomic shocks at business cycle frequencies. The method extends existing functional VAR models by "looking within" the micro distribution to identify the degree to which specific types of micro units are affected by macro shocks. It does so by creating a pseudo-panel from the repeated cross-section and adding these pseudo individuals into the macro VAR. Jointly modeling the micro and macro data leads to a large (pseudo) VAR, and we use Bayesian methods to ensure shrinkage and parsimony. Our application revisits Chang et al. (2024) and compares their functional VAR-based distributional impulse response functions with our proposed pseudo VAR-based ones to identify what types of individuals' earnings are most affected by business-cycle-type shocks. We find that the individuals exhibiting the strongest positive cyclical sensitivity are those in the lower tail of the earnings distribution, particularly men and those without a college education, as well as young workers.

detail.abstract: Data science and big data offer many opportunities for researchers, not only in the domain of data science and related sciences, but also for researchers in many other disciplines. The fact that data science and big data are playing an increasingly important role in so many research areas raises the question whether this also applies to the legal domain. Do data science and big data also offer methods of data research for law? As will be shown in this chapter, the answer to this question is positive: yes, there are many methods and applications that may be also useful for the legal domain. This answer will be provided by discussing these methods of data research for law in this chapter. As such, this chapter provides an overview of these methods.

title: The New Frontiers of Legal Evaluation
affiliations: Leiden University - Center for Law and Digital Technologies

detail.title: The New Frontiers of Legal Evaluation

publicationDetails.detailsText: Artificial Intelligence and Big data: Lessons from Evaluations of the Rule of Law and Development, Cheltenham UK: Edgar Elgar.

detail.abstract: This chapter focuses on the new frontiers of evaluation, with a focus on the field of law. After briefly setting the stage with some background on how new sources of data and automated data analytics can contribute to evaluations and the field of evaluation studies, the focus is turned to how these developments in big data and data science can influence individuals and society. Although the use of big data, data science, and AI has many benefits, there are also serious issues and concerns, including many sources of bias and issues of data quality, as well as risks of cybercrime. Other concerns are that sometimes correlations and causality are confused and that some (but obviously not all) researchers believe that working with very large datasets will eliminate, or at least reduce, bias. This chapter will dig into these pros and cons of these new approaches, including several examples.

title: Corporate Political Revelation and Consumer Demand: Evidence from a Natural Experiment
affiliations: University of Houston - C.T. Bauer College of Business and University of Notre Dame

detail.title: Corporate Political Revelation and Consumer Demand: Evidence from a Natural Experiment
detail.abstract: We study how corporate political revelation, defined as the externally driven disclosure of a firm’s political association, affects consumer demand. Using data from a large U.S.-based lifestyle specialty retail brand and a comparable control brand, we exploit a natural experiment in which the focal brand’s political association was involuntarily revealed by a third party. We find that the focal brand’s sales increase by 17.1% in dollar amount and 12.7% in quantity over the 11 weeks following the disclosure relative to the control brand. The sales response emerges shortly after the revelation, is concentrated in the first several post-event weeks, and attenuates thereafter. Sales responses are heterogeneous across locations, with larger effects in counties whose political preferences align more closely with the brand’s revealed association and no aggregate sales decline in misaligned locations. Decomposing the response, we show that the increase in sales operates primarily through the extensive margin, reflected in higher customer participation rather than greater spending per customer. Finally, category-level analyses reveal that political-alignment-based heterogeneity is concentrated in conspicuous, rather than inconspicuous, products. This finding is consistent with an identity-signaling mechanism whereby CPR shapes consumer behavior by encouraging politically aligned consumers to express their identities through publicly visible consumption.

title: Structural Admissibility of Asset Price Trajectories: A Theoretical Price-Only Effective Action Framework
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Structural Admissibility of Asset Price Trajectories: A Theoretical Price-Only Effective Action Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is a principal at Aregis LLC [and SagaHalla], which engages in proprietary trading and risk management. The theoretical framework described in this paper is utilized in the firm’s investment and risk governance activities. No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: Abstract Modern financial markets exhibit regime shifts, instability, and path-dependent behavior that challenge prediction-centric modeling approaches. While extensive literature exists on forecasting and stochastic diffusion, comparatively little attention has been given to formal criteria for determining when observed price dynamics remain structurally admissible under evolving conditions. This paper introduces a theoretical price-only effective action framework for diagnosing the structural admissibility of asset price trajectories. Formulated entirely in discrete time using observable price series, the framework decomposes price dynamics into three orthogonal integrity dimensions: Material (geometric coherence), Energetic (volatility stability), and Temporal (directional persistence). These dimensions act as phenomenological constraint fields that condition admissible trajectories without generating or predicting price movements. An “effective action” is defined as the cumulative aggregation of integrity-conditioned contributions along a realized price path. High action values correspond to structural incoherence and repeated constraint violations, while low action values indicate compatibility with recent market structure. We propose a dissipation-conditioned energetic term with a scale-matching attenuation constant, estimated through stability criteria rather than performance optimization. The framework is presented not as a predictive tool, but as a structural diagnostic for “disciplined abstention”—identifying when market conditions preclude structural coherence. We conclude by outlining a set of falsifiable hypotheses to guide future empirical validation.

title: Functional Penalized Ridge Regression with a Parametric Partitioning Framework for High-Dimensional Data
affiliations: Lund University, Quaid i Azam University and Quaid i Azam University

detail.title: Functional Penalized Ridge Regression with a Parametric Partitioning Framework for High-Dimensional Data
detail.abstract: This study proposes a novel partition-based functional ridge regression framework to address key challenges in functional linear models, including multicollinearity, overfitting, and interpretability. The coefficient function vector β(s) is partitioned into relevant β 1 (s) and nuisance β 2 (s) components, enabling selective penalization that distinguishes structurally important effects from redundant or weak signals. The proposed partitioning strategy serves as the key mechanism for adaptive penalization in the functional ridge framework. This partitioning allows the model to adaptively control regularization strength across different components of the functional covariates which is an essential step in high-dimensional settings where irrelevant functional predictors can inflate variance and obscure interpretability. Our proposed estimators, the Functional Ridge Estimator (FRE), the Functional Ridge Full Model (FRFM), and the Functional Ridge Sub-Model (FRSM), apply tailored ridge penalties (λ 1 , λ 2 , λ 3) to regulate smoothness and shrinkage. Under standard regularity conditions, the estimators are shown to be consistent, asymptotically normal, and efficient. Monte Carlo experiments confirm that FRSM yields the lowest Integrated mean squared error (IMSE) in small samples, while FRFM offers greater stability for moderate and large samples. An empirical application to Canadian weather data further validates the framework, demonstrating reduced variance inflation and improved interpretability.

title: The Risk Sensitivity of Global Liquidity Flows: Heterogeneity, Evolution and Drivers
affiliations: Bank for International Settlements (BIS), Bank for International Settlements (BIS), Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Bank of Italy

detail.title: The Risk Sensitivity of Global Liquidity Flows: Heterogeneity, Evolution and Drivers

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 973
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The period after the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) was characterized by a considerable risk migration within global liquidity flows, away from cross-border bank lending towards international bond issuance. We show that the post-GFC shifts in the risk sensitivities of global liquidity flows are related to the tightness of the (capital and liquidity) constraints faced by international (bank and non-bank) lenders and to the migration of borrowers across funding sources. We show that the risk sensitivity of global liquidity flows is higher when funding is provided by financial intermediaries that are facing greater balance sheet (capital and leverage) constraints. We also provide evidence that the post-GFC migration of borrowers from cross-border loans towards international debt securities was associated with a decline in the risk sensitivity of global liquidity flows and their main components.

title: IGD-OS: An Architectural Framework for Synchronizing Institutional Will (SBR-I) and Economic Resources (SBR-E) to Optimize National Performance in Emerging Markets

detail.title: IGD-OS: An Architectural Framework for Synchronizing Institutional Will (SBR-I) and Economic Resources (SBR-E) to Optimize National Performance in Emerging Markets
detail.abstract:
In developing and transitional economics, the primary paradox of growth lies not in resources scarcity, but in the “dynamic asynchrony” between the superstructure (Institutions) and the infrastructure (Economy). Traditional public governance models imported from the West often fail in these context because they predicate on a “frictionless” environment, overlooking the idiosyncrasies of nations where the State retains a dominant role in resource allocation.

This paper introduces a novel empirical governance doctrine: the Institutional Governance Dynamic Operating System (IGD-OS). Moving beyond qualitative policy analysis, IGD-OS models the nation-state as a mechanical apparatus comprising two primary gear systems requiring precise interlocking:

1-      SBR-I (State-Based Resources – Institutional): Represents the Drive Gear, encapsulating political will, legislative authority, and steering mechanism.

2-      SBR-E (State-Based Resources – Economics): Represent the Driven Gear, encompassing natural capital, strategic infrastructure, and fiscal flows.

Utilizing the quantitative formula , the study isolates two critical retarding variables: Dynamic Friction (), arising from procedural overlap, and Integrity Noise (, stemming from information opacity.

The core thesis posits that sustainable prosperity derives not from the chaotic liberalization of SBR-I to synchronize its velocity and vector with SBR-E. The research propose a paradigm shift from “Administrative Command” to “Real-time Parameter Control”, leveraging data to neutralize friction and maximize the efficiency of resource conversion.

Distilled from empirical supply chain operations in Vietnam, IGD-OS offers an engineering solution to the middle-income trap, providing a robust framework for synchronizing political objectives with market dynamics.

title: Politics will Tear us Apart, Again. Geopolitical Risk, Fragmentation, and Capital Flows
affiliations: Bank of Italy

detail.title: Politics will Tear us Apart, Again. Geopolitical Risk, Fragmentation, and Capital Flows

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 974
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This review summarizes empirical research on the impact that geopolitical risk and financial fragmentation have on cross-border capital flows. It distinguishes between event-driven geopolitical risk and structural political divides, showing that both affect international investment through retrenchment and alignment-based reallocation. Using gravity models, the literature documents how political distance increasingly shapes foreign direct investment and portfolio flows, particularly into emerging markets, strategic sectors, and, to some extent in the euro area following the invasion of Ukraine. Open questions include the macroeconomic consequences of financial fragmentation, its impact on the global financial cycle, and the implications for the role of reserve currencies.

title: Is there a Tech Bubble in the US Stock Market? Evidence from an Agnostic Valuation Procedure
affiliations: Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy and Banca d’Italia

detail.title: Is there a Tech Bubble in the US Stock Market? Evidence from an Agnostic Valuation Procedure

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 975
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We propose an agnostic procedure for deriving implied abnormal earnings growth rates from equity prices. We use a dividend discount model that requires minimal subjective inputs, as its parameters are constrained by equilibrium conditions and can be estimated by the generalized method of moments using historical data. We use the model to address the debate on the potential overvaluation of large US technology companies involved in the Artificial Intelligence race. We compute the abnormal growth rates of earnings that would justify their current equity valuations, i.e., that would make them compatible with rational pricing in line with historical norms. We find that the current valuations would be rational if technology firms were able to sustain expansion rates for earnings that, while high, do not seem implausible given historical experience and the structural drivers of future growth.

title: Structural Liquidity Traps: Micro-Economic Consumption Inefficiency and Solvency Distress in Urban Java's Aspiring Class

detail.title: Structural Liquidity Traps: Micro-Economic Consumption Inefficiency and Solvency Distress in Urban Java's Aspiring Class

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. This research was conducted independently and the views expressed are solely those of the author.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study relies exclusively on the synthesis of secondary data sources (BPS, OJK, LPS) and aggregated public pricing data from retail platforms. No personally identifiable information (PII) was collected, and no direct experimentation on human subjects was conducted. Therefore, formal ethics committee approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Despite robust aggregate growth (5% GDP), Indonesia's "Aspiring Class" (115-137 million individuals) faces a structural solvency crisis, marked by a contraction of the middle class by 9.5 million people (BPS, 2025). This paper investigates the microeconomic drivers of this divergence, proposing that supply chain inefficiencies impose a regressive "Quantity Surcharge" (Sachet Premium) on liquidity-constrained households. Using Aggregated Real-Time Pricing data from Urban Java in Q4 2025, and controlling for unemployment and wage growth, this study identifies a persistent regressive cost structure. Findings indicate that liquidity-constrained households pay a risk-adjusted premium of 32-35% for non-perishable necessities compared to wealthier cohorts. Sensitivity analysis confirms that this premium persists even under high-risk storage assumptions (> 20%). Furthermore, panel data suggests a significant positive correlation (β = 0.34) between Volatile Food Inflation and Fintech Default Rates (TWP90). The paper argues that supply chain inefficiencies function as an implicit regressive tax, forcing households to substitute savings with high-interest consumption credit. I propose "Supply Chain Aggregation" and "Whitelisted Inventory Financing" as superior policy alternatives to unbridled credit expansion.

title: Empirical Validation of Structural Admissibility in Asset Price Trajectories
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Empirical Validation of Structural Admissibility in Asset Price Trajectories

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the research presented in this paper. This work is presented as independent academic research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Financial markets are characterized by persistent non-stationarity, regime dependence, and intermittent structural breakdowns, challenging approaches that prioritize prediction or optimization. In a companion theoretical work, we introduced structural admissibility as a diagnostic property of realized price trajectories, defined by their compatibility with internally inferred integrity constraints rather than forecast accuracy. This paper provides an empirical validation of the admissibility framework. Using only daily closing prices, we evaluate realized trajectories across a heterogeneous universe of 25 assets spanning cryptocurrencies, equities, indices, and commodities. We test three falsifiable hypotheses: (i) that realized price paths exhibit statistically distinguishable admissibility relative to randomized surrogates; (ii) that energetic integrity encodes time-varying structural capacity with horizondependent relationships to future volatility; and (iii) that the dissipation attenuation parameter behaves as a stable structural quantity rather than a fitted artifact. We find that admissibility is neither trivial nor universal. A subset of assets occupies systematically lower-action regimes than surrogate trajectories, energetic integrity exhibits short-horizon relationships to future volatility that decay over time without requiring elevated contemporaneous volatility, and dissipation parameters remain stable for structurally coherent assets while degrading under instability. Importantly, null results are informative rather than pathological, delineating environments where participation is structurally unsupported. Collectively, these findings establish admissibility as a meaningful and measurable structural diagnostic, distinct from predictive or performance-driven frameworks. By elevating abstention and structural failure to informative outcomes, the admissibility framework provides an empirical foundation for subsequent decision, allocation, and governance layers without prescribing them.

title: After-Arising Technologies and the Written Description Requirement -'Functional Claiming without Structural Anchor': Lessons from the Entresto Patent Case for India
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: After-Arising Technologies and the Written Description Requirement -'Functional Claiming without Structural Anchor': Lessons from the Entresto Patent Case for India
detail.abstract: The splendour of interpretation of patent rests upon the eyes of a litigant. When the world believed that the litigants had done all they could in the interpretation of the patent, and now nothing remains to challenge the nature of patent jurisprudence, they were proved again wrong. The case of Entresto in the United States demonstrates that speed in scientific development usually surpasses the law vocabulary and demonstrates opposition between legal confidence and science. The case of Novartis v. HEC Pharma of United States brought up the issues of the after-arising technologies and adequacy of the patents. The case restated that an invention specification should be detailed enough ot cover the invention as it is filed and cannot respond on the scientific knowledge that will be developed later to keep the invention alive and this bega the question, should the law of patent not be adaptable to future technological progress or is ti just limited to what is currently enabled. The case points out the fact that it is not the case that what is covered in the claims and how it is construed, but rather what the claims actually say, which also brings about tension between broad claims and coverage at a later stage. Entresto case, is a grave worry to the biotech companies, particularly to those in the early-stage innovations, as they may now find it challenging during scrutiny or in the court and may lead to a change in future business practises. In the case of biotech especially where the formulations, delivery systems, complexes, prodrugs, cell types or methods could change at a very high rate, drafting would still need to be progressive. Entresto can be construed in any manner and another cross-jursidictional gap on patent jurisprudence exists. In India, the same is provided under Sections 10 and 64 of the Patent Act, 1970, where full and fair disclosure is mandatory, the claims should be narrow, in accordance with the US patent jurisprudence. Neverthless, with the improvements in biopharmaceutical research, gene therapy, and AI-based drug discovery, the scales of disclosure adequacy and technological dynamism are becoming all the more fine. This paper examines the implications of the Entresto decision as it seeks to redefine the global discussions on the adequacy of patents and offers the possible solution to the current patent jurisprudence in India as the country seeks to develop its biotechnology sector.

title: Outlook for Korea's 13 Flagship Industries in 2026

detail.title: Outlook for Korea's 13 Flagship Industries in 2026

publicationDetails.detailsText: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade Research Paper No. 25/IER/30/06/02
publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics & Trade Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: KIET Industrial Economic Review Vol. 30 No. 6, pp. 20-34

detail.abstract: In 2026, South Korea's 13 flagship industries are expected to follow divergent paths against a backdrop of moderate global growth, a slow recovery in world trade, and accelerating technological change. The information technology (IT) and emerging industries sectors-comprising the semiconductors, information and communications technology (ICT) devices, secondary batteries, and biohealth industries-are projected to lead growth on the back of strong demand for artificial intelligence (AI) and electric vehicles (EV), while growth in the machinery sectors (automobiles, ships, general machinery) should pick back up slightly. Growth in the materials sectors (steel, petrochemicals, refined oil, textiles) looks to remain subdued amid slack external demand and China's newfound self-sufficiency in materials production. Korea's export portfolio is likely to become more concentrated than ever in high value-added IT and biohealth products, while shipments of materials and general machinery stay weak or even contract.

title: Korean Economic Outlook for 2026

detail.title: Korean Economic Outlook for 2026

publicationDetails.detailsText: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics and Trade Research Paper No. 25/IER/30/06/01
publicationDetails.journalName: Korea Institute for Industrial Economics & Trade Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: KIET Industrial Economic Review Vol. 30, No. 6, pp. 6-19

detail.abstract: Korea's economy is projected to grow by 1.9 percent in 2026, with domestic demand serving as the primary engine of expansion. Private consumption is expected to rise by 1.7 percent, as inflation stabilizes, interest rates fall, real incomes grow, and the government pursues expansionary fiscal policy. Facility investment is forecast to continue its upward trend, driven by improved financing conditions and strong investment demand in hightech industries related to artificial intelligence (AI). Construction investment is expected to finally rebound; we anticipate an uptick of 2.7 percent, marking the first positive growth in this metric since 2020, largely due to higher government spending on social overhead capital (SOC). Exports are projected to decline by 0.5 percent amid weak global growth, subdued trade activity, and a high base effect, while US tariff risks and ongoing US-China tensions will remain key external headwinds. Imports are expected to fall by 0.3 percent, reflecting weaker intermediate goods demand and lower import prices. We forecast the trade surplus to be USD 67.5 billion, representing a slight decline from 2025. International oil prices are expected to fall due to persistent oversupply and weak demand growth. The KRW-USD exchange rate is projected to average around 1,391 won to the dollar, with appreciation of the won constrained by uncertainties surrounding further US rate cuts.

title: The Collision between Foreign Investment and Human Rights in the Host Country
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Collision between Foreign Investment and Human Rights in the Host Country
detail.abstract:
The interplay of various economic, political, and historic factors has shaped the development of international laws of foreign investment. International Investment Law is an area in which the interests of capital exporting states have clashed with those of capital importing states, reflecting environmental, labour, indigenous, cultural, property and other rights. Thus, the International Investment Law illustrates the intense conflicts between businesses, social and national interests. On the other hand, human rights also reflect a collision between investment interest and social and corporate responsibilities.

       As a consequence, there has been increased debate about the limited scope of human rights in International Investment Arbitration. The main reason for this is that international investment tribunals have a completely different regime. They tend to reject the host state’s right in favour of foreign investor’s protection, as the investment should be protected under the International Investment Law. Hence, human rights come in indirect manner to the core of issues related with investment.

       From this perspective, this paper aims to analyse problems arising with the human rights protection by foreign investment. It presents the main actors and the different scenarios by the interaction between investment and human rights protection and explores how international investment tribunals consider human rights issues. Furthermore, the article reveals the possibilities for legal remedies as well as the options for human rights protection that could be implemented by host countries. The most important conclusions of the paper as well as further possible developments are summarised at the end.

title: Cripto-FUD: Ontological Death in the Form of Stability
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Cripto-FUD: Ontological Death in the Form of Stability
detail.abstract: The essay "Crypto-Absurdity" describes a symptom: an autoimmune failure of a system attacking its own resources. This is a precise, almost clinical diagnosis, yet it remains within the pathological paradigm-a framework that views the crypto-system merely as a pathology within a social organism. However, when a pathology becomes total and its symptoms turn into systemic invariants, the diagnosis demands a shift in perspective. NOW we must take the next step: to recognize not just the disease, but the nature of the being for which such a "disease" is the only possible mode of existence, and the described "symptoms" are its essential and necessary features.

title: Gender Wage Gap Across the Income Distribution: Evidence from Central Asia
affiliations: Maqsut Narikbayev University and Maqsut Narikbayev University

detail.title: Gender Wage Gap Across the Income Distribution: Evidence from Central Asia
detail.abstract: This paper examines the magnitude and distribution of the gender wage gap in Central Asia, a region that combines features of developing and transition economies yet remains largely understudied. Using data from the Life in Transition Survey IV, we estimate wage differentials within a Mincerian earnings framework employing ordinary least squares, Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition, and Heckman selection models to account for nonrandom labor market participation. To analyze heterogeneity across the wage distribution, we apply quantile regression and the Chernozhukov-Fernández-Val-Melly decomposition method. The results reveal substantial crosscountry heterogeneity in gender wage inequality. Kazakhstan exhibits a pronounced glass-ceiling effect, with gender wage gaps increasing toward the upper tail of the wage distribution. In other countries, wage gaps emerge mainly at the middle and upper quantiles and are largely driven by coefficient effects. In less developed economies, gender inequality operates primarily through labor market participation rather than wage differentials among employed workers. This pattern is particularly evident in Tajikistan and Uzbekistan, while for the Kyrgyz Republic we find no robust evidence of systematic gender wage inequality. Overall, the findings highlight that both the extent and the mechanisms of gender inequality differ markedly across Central Asian labor markets.

title: Bread or Circuses? The Conundrum of Non-Contingent Clientelism and the Informal Economy
affiliations: Department of Political Science, Yale University

detail.title: Bread or Circuses? The Conundrum of Non-Contingent Clientelism and the Informal Economy
detail.abstract: High inequality in developing democracies is frequently associated with a decline in programmatic politics and a rise in vote buying, a contradiction of standard median-voter predictions. This article explains this divergence by modeling the political logic of the "dual economy". Using a Global Games framework, I demonstrate that in contexts with large informal sectors, incumbents are structurally incentivised to trade regressive policy concessions for elite campaign contributions. These funds are deployed not as targeted patronage, but as high-visibility "viability signals". For informal voters, who inhabit a paralegal existence dependent on state forbearance, these signals resolve a crucial coordination problem by identifying the dominant patron. Testing this mechanism against cross-national data, experimental evidence from the Philippines, and post-socialist transition cases, the analysis suggests that the substitution of redistribution with electioneering is a rational response to the fiscal logic of informality, rather than a result of voter myopia.

title: Quantifying Climate Risk Premia
affiliations: EDHEC Business School and EDHEC Business School

detail.title: Quantifying Climate Risk Premia
detail.abstract: What are the quantifiable financial risks of climate change? We present a fully calibrated, literature-and policy-aligned framework linking a climate module with a workhorse asset-pricing model. It uniquely integrates transition risks tied to climate policy, physical risks reflecting persistent but not permanent impacts beyond adaptation, and the structural feedback from economic activity to temperature. Our framework yields closed-form solutions for time-varying risk-free rates, equity risk premia, and price-dividend ratios. In contrast to the existing long-run risks climate asset-pricing literature, we show that chronic climate risks generate positive risk premia, even without tipping points, increasing the equity risk premium by nearly 20% under 3°C of warming, which is sufficient to anticipate substantial market repricing.

title: The Macroeconomic Effects of Neighborhood Policies: a Dynamic Analysis
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis, University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, NERA Economic Consulting and Bocconi University

detail.title: The Macroeconomic Effects of Neighborhood Policies: a Dynamic Analysis

publicationDetails.detailsText: NBER Working Paper No. w34754
publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We study the macroeconomic effects of neighborhood-specific policies in a general equilibrium model of a city with endogenous residential sorting and educational investment. A key feature of the model is the presence of endogenous local spillovers that depend on the distribution of families across neighborhoods. We analyze three policies: a housing-voucher policy inspired by the MTO program, which enables poor families to relocate to low-poverty neighborhoods; a place-based transfer (PBT) policy that provides monetary transfers to families in poor neighborhoods; and a place-based investment (PBI) policy that invests resources in local institutions, such as public schools, to directly enhance local spillovers. We find that the MTO policy generates substantial income gains for children of recipient families, but scaling up the program dampens these gains and induces large welfare losses for non-recipients. By contrast, the PBT policy delivers larger average welfare gains but is less effective in reducing inequality and segregation. Finally, the PBI policy produces smaller short-run effects but, over time, resolves the trade-off by raising average welfare while simultaneously reducing inequality, lowering segregation, and improving intergenerational mobility.
