title: Protest Matters: The Effects of Protests on Economic Redistribution
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University, Harvard University, Covenant University - Department of Economics & Development Studies and Columbia University

detail.title: Protest Matters: The Effects of Protests on Economic Redistribution

publicationDetails.detailsText: NBER Working Paper No. w34787
publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Can citizen-led protests lead to meaningful economic redistribution and nudge governments to increase redistributive fiscal transfers? We study the effects of protests on fiscal redistribution using evidence from Nigeria. We digitized twenty-six years of public finance data from 1988 to 2016 to examine the effects of protests on intergovernmental transfers. We find that protests increase transfers to protesting regions, but only in areas that are politically aligned with disbursing governments. Evidence from the large-scale 2012 Occupy Nigeria protests confirms these results. Protesters also face increased police violence, particularly in non-aligned regions. The results show that protests can influence fiscal redistribution.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Social Security Code 2020: Social Protection for Informal and Unorganised Workers under the New Labour Law
affiliations: National Law School of India University

detail.title: Social Security Code 2020: Social Protection for Informal and Unorganised Workers under the New Labour Law
detail.abstract: India’s workforce is largely informal, with the rapid expansion of gig and platform work reshaping traditional employment structures. The Code on Social Security, 2020 represents a major legislative attempt to extend social protection to unorganised, gig and platform workers through a consolidated legal framework. This paper examines whether the Code delivers substantive social security or merely symbolic inclusion through discretionary, scheme-based mechanisms. It analyses key provisions relating to definitions, welfare boards, funding, registration and schemes, while highlighting their implications for gig workers, platform workers, domestic workers and other vulnerable groups. Although the Code broadens coverage and introduces institutional and digital mechanisms such as registration and aggregator contributions, it does not confer enforceable, right-based entitlements and continues to exclude gig and platform workers from employee status. The paper argues that effective social protection requires compulsory contributions, clearer liability frameworks and a shift from employment-centric welfare to livelihood-oriented social security.

title: Optimal Managerial Contracting with Investment and Abandonment Decisions
affiliations: and University of Porto, School of Economics and Management

detail.title: Optimal Managerial Contracting with Investment and Abandonment Decisions

contentType.other: Paper submitted for publication and under review

detail.abstract: This paper develops a dynamic compensation scheme that aligns the incentives of a shareholder and a manager, who sequentially decides when to invest in and when to abandon a project. Unlike the existing literature, our framework specifies all contractual parameters ex ante, without subsequent revision of the sharing rule. The model determines the optimal severance payment, sharing rate, and fixed wages that jointly align the investment and abandonment thresholds, resulting in a credible and time-consistent contract. We further examine how behavioral distortions in managerial attitudes toward adverse conditions, distinguishing between fair-weather and persistent managers, affect project abandonment and how the optimal contract can neutralize such biases.

title: Disclosure in Hosted Design Contests

detail.title: Disclosure in Hosted Design Contests
detail.abstract: This paper studies contests in which contestants with different designs compete via effort to win a prize from the host of the competition. The host's ideal design is her private information, which she can disclose to the contestants before they choose their effort levels. We investigate how the host's disclosure policy affects the effort choices of contestants when her objective is to maximize aggregate effort. We find that non-disclosure leads to symmetric equilibria while disclosure induces asymmetry. We derive equilibrium effort levels with and without disclosure and identify a threshold prize value above which disclosure yields a higher aggregate effort.

title: When Biased Beliefs Lead to Optimal Action: An Experimental Study
affiliations: Texas A&M University - Department of Economics and Korea Information Society Development Institute (KISDI)

detail.title: When Biased Beliefs Lead to Optimal Action: An Experimental Study
detail.abstract: Incorrectly assessing a team member’s ability—whether overestimating or underestimating—can lead to inefficient task allocation. Using a series of laboratory experiments, we show that allocative inefficiencies can be mitigated when an institution is designed such that overall productivity depends on aggregates of individual productivities rather than each individual's productivity. When evaluating a group’s overall productivity, errors in beliefs about individual abilities tend to offset each other, reducing their distorting impact on task allocation. Our findings support the theory of misspecified learning (e.g., Heidhues et al., 2018) and offer insights into designing institutions that prevent belief biases from translating into economic inefficiencies.

title: Estimating Experienced Inequality: A Rank-Weighted Generated Regressor with Application to Health

detail.title: Estimating Experienced Inequality: A Rank-Weighted Generated Regressor with Application to Health
detail.abstract: I propose a new latent individual-level measure of experienced inequality motivated by the relative income hypothesis which is substantial to health economics, and develop a kernel-based generated-regressor estimator for this object, together with large-sample theory and inference for its effect on health within a concave income-health production framework. The proposed measure treats experienced inequality as a smooth rank-weighted functional of the income distribution that aggregates proximity-weighted social comparisons in percentile space, allowing the salience of income gaps and sensitivity to comparisons to vary across the distribution. This definition yields an estimand that is conceptually aligned with social-comparison models but fundamentally distinct from conventional scalar inequality indices. I show how the latent functional can be estimated by a rank-based plug-in procedure that replaces the unknown income distribution with its empirical counterpart. The resulting covariate is a nonlinear statistic of the full sample and therefore a generated regressor. I establish uniform consistency, asymptotic linearity, and asymptotic normality of the estimator, and derive valid inference for the health effect parameter that explicitly accounts for first-stage estimation error. I also outline a cross-fitted, data-driven procedure for selecting comparison primitives within a finite, interpretable class. Monte Carlo experiments demonstrate that the proposed estimator accurately recovers experienced inequality in finite samples and delivers reliable inference, while regressions using standard global inequality measures suffer persistent attenuation bias when the true mechanism operates through local social comparisons. I further discuss how the framework integrates with standard identification strategies, including IV/2SLS designs, and how it can be adapted to common applied complications such as income measurement error and non-random sampling. The paper introduces a new class of individual-level rank-weighted distributional functionals and corresponding estimators, expanding the econometric toolkit for studying outcomes that depend on individuals' positions within distributions, with applications to health, status, relative deprivation, and peer effects.

title: Taxing Beta, Exempting Alpha: A Benchmark-Based Inheritance Regime

detail.title: Taxing Beta, Exempting Alpha: A Benchmark-Based Inheritance Regime

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a generational benchmark inheritance regime as a structural replacement for the federal estate tax. By distinguishing between systemic market returns (Beta) and active value creation (Alpha), the regime captures the passive growth of capital at generational boundaries while fully exempting idiosyncratic surplus. Using a Pareto tail interpolation (α ≈ 1.163) calibrated to Federal Reserve wealth data, we estimate baseline annual revenue of approximately $295 billion under conservative assumptions. This revenue is sufficient to finance a 2.1 percentage point reduction in the OASDI payroll tax, shifting the fiscal burden from labor to underperforming dynastic capital. Unlike continuous wealth taxes, the regime requires no new valuation machinery, relying exclusively on existing estate and gift tax procedures. We situate the proposal within the Jeffersonian principle of usufruct and the modern literature on optimal inheritance taxation.

title: Investor Distraction and Multi-Dimensional Financial Narrative
affiliations: Bocconi University - Department of Accounting, Bocconi University - Department of Accounting and Vanderbilt University - Finance

detail.title: Investor Distraction and Multi-Dimensional Financial Narrative

publicationDetails.detailsText: Review of Accounting Studies, forthcoming

detail.abstract: This paper investigates how institutional investor distraction affects the assimilation of narrative content in the MD&A section of the 10-K filing. We introduce the Aggregate Attribute Index (AAI) and an alternative formulation (AltAAI), which capture linguistic features beyond tone to provide a broader measure of corporate narrative richness. Using machine learning and natural language processing, we analyze U.S. firms that follow a staggered reporting strategy, releasing quantitative results before full narrative disclosures. This design isolates the incremental effects of complex language when other portfolio events distract investors. We find that narrative complexity does not trigger short-term return responses but significantly affects stock prices over longer horizons. Complexity moderates how and when attention-constrained investors adjust prices. These effects are not captured by dictionary-based tone or readability metrics, underscoring the distinct role of multi-dimensional attributes in shaping delayed market reactions and price discovery.

title: Microfoundations of the Cultural Modernization Theory
affiliations: National Research University – Higher School of Economics (HSE University) and National Research University – Higher School of Economics (HSE University)

detail.title: Microfoundations of the Cultural Modernization Theory

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There are no interests to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: This article was prepared within the framework of the Basic Research Program at HSE University.

detail.abstract: This paper attempts to model the evolutionary theory of modernization and democratization. The model reflects the key provisions of R. Inglehart and C. Welzel's theory and provides a microfoundation for the adaptation of subjective values to the objective importances of the survival factors and the structure of the labour markets from the perspective of evolutionary theory and rational-emotional choice. We consider an optimization problem of a representative agent allocating their time between production of private goods (participation in the economy), distribution of public goods (participation in politics), and leisure. Thus, the long-term dynamics of the allocation of society's time resources can be explained by technological progress (reduction in the labour intensity of production), social progress (increasing effectiveness of political institutions), and structural changes in the labour markets (altering importances of work, politics, and leisure). In addition, the model developed in the paper reflects the phenomenon of hedonic adaptation and the resulting Easterlin paradox, explains the modern trend towards a higher share of the government in the economy, and illustrates the democratic congruence theory by C. Welzel. The key implications of the model are tested against data from the WVS/EVS and other sources.

title: Overnight Returns, Trading Constraints, and Future Stock Returns: Evidence from the Chinese A-Share Market
affiliations: Xiamen University - Department of Finance, Xiamen University and Victoria University of Wellington - Te Herenga Waka - School of Economics & Finance

detail.title: Overnight Returns, Trading Constraints, and Future Stock Returns: Evidence from the Chinese A-Share Market

declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 72371210).

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the differential predictive power of overnight and intraday returns in China's A-share market. We find that overnight returns exhibit a significantly positive and robust relation with future stock returns at intermediate horizons, whereas intraday returns display no comparable predictive effect. Mechanism analysis indicates that this predictability is primarily driven by the T+1 trading rule, which restricts timely selling and leads to an underreaction to negative information. Further analyses show that overnight returns embed information about future earnings, suggesting that they capture the delayed incorporation of fundamental news resulting from institutional trading frictions. Our findings differ from patterns documented in developed markets and offer new insights into the price discovery process in emerging equity markets.

title: Technoversal Leadership for Biodiversity and Climate

detail.title: Technoversal Leadership for Biodiversity and Climate
detail.abstract: This work brings a holistic perspective to business leadership, environment, biodiversity, and climate interactions. In light of historical facts, business leaders must get involved in biodiversity loss and climate change to rectify them. And to solve these problems, environmental consciousness, biodiversity, and climate must urgently be one of the core elements of leadership. Along with accomplishing the goal of protecting nature and sustaining biodiversity, leaders are also obliged to meet business objectives. And to achieve them together, it is necessary to bring a well defined framework to leadership qualities that leaders must possess. And readers will find these mostly-needed vital behaviors, skills, and qualities inside. In the framework of examples from leadership history, the author coins the term T-Leaders, which stands for Transactional, Transformational, and Technoversal Leader. The author also gives place to some other concepts and styles that he contributed to the literature: APARTS Behaviors, Self-Created-Problem-Solution Cycle, DOER Behaviors, DOER Leader, Big Ten of Leadership, Gold Medalist Behaviors, Silver Medalist Behaviors.

title: Capital-Consumption Theory: Productivity Growth, Income Synchronization, and the Macroeconomics of Abundance
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Capital-Consumption Theory: Productivity Growth, Income Synchronization, and the Macroeconomics of Abundance
detail.abstract:
This paper develops a demand-constrained macroeconomic framework in which productivity growth, income distribution, and aggregate demand jointly determine capacity utilization. The economy is modeled as two functional sectors-worker-consumers, whose wage income sustains demand, and capital owners, whose investment expands productive capacity-producing output via partially substitutable labor and technological capital. 

The central mechanism is a wage-demand feedback loop: wages generate demand, and demand sustains wages. When productivity gains accrue primarily to capital, labor demand weakens, wages stagnate, and productive capacity expands faster than consumption, generating persistent underutilization even alongside output and productivity growth. When income flows to households keep pace with labor-only productivity, demand and utilization remain synchronized, supporting sustained expansion. 

The framework interprets historical growth and stagnation phases as emergent outcomes of this synchronization dynamic and applies the model to the contemporary acceleration of technological capital, including artificial intelligence. The analysis highlights broad income mechanisms-such as universal transfers or widespread capital participation-as macroeconomic instruments capable of stabilizing demand in high-productivity economies.

title: Firm-Level Uncertainty and Output Prices
affiliations: Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: Firm-Level Uncertainty and Output Prices

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 966
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Based on the unique information provided by Banca d’Italia’s Survey on Inflation and Growth Expectations, we develop an indicator of firm-level ex ante uncertainty on future business conditions and use it to estimate the relationship between uncertainty and the expected development of each firm’s selling prices. We find evidence that price flexibility increases with uncertainty: firms facing uncertainty both show a higher propensity to introduce price changes in the following months (extensive margin) and to make larger price changes compared with the other firms (intensive margin). This evidence suggests that price stickiness may ease in times of high uncertainty.

title: From Unified Discounting to Dual-Risk: A New Lens on DCF Valuation
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: From Unified Discounting to Dual-Risk: A New Lens on DCF Valuation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.

declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently, without external funding or institutional support.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Finance Research Open, 2026[10.1016/j.finr.2026.100096]

detail.abstract: Traditional discounted cash-flow (DCF) valuation often compresses uncertainty into a single discount rate. This blends two conceptually distinct objects: an external opportunity cost for priced risk and time, and belief-driven distortion in cash-flow (benefit) expectations. As a result, a valuation gap cannot be attributed cleanly to priced premia versus forecast distortion. We formalize this identification problem across common implementations, including CAPM-based discounting, WACC-plus-premium rules, and implied-cost approaches. We also argue that discounting often becomes self-referential in practice: when required-return inputs are inferred from, calibrated to, or primarily validated by the same market prices they are meant to benchmark, the opportunity-cost interpretation of discounting is violated. We develop a dual-risk framework with two primitives: a market-based cost of capital c and a valuation ratio K that captures distortion in expected benefits relative to a benchmark. The wedge captured by K can arise from forecast error, disagreement, informational frictions, behavioral distortions, or model misspecification, and it may be persistent or transitory. From (c, K) we derive the ex-ante gain of capital g and an effective hurdle rate c_eff , decomposing expected return into benchmark discounting and expectation distortion. A parsimonious market-clearing equilibrium clarifies how heterogeneous wedges K can persist in prices under belief heterogeneity and limits to arbitrage. We then propose a proxying scheme for c and K from observable total-return prices given a chosen benchmark rate, and illustrate it on equity (VTI), gold (GLD), and Bitcoin (BTC-USD), where non-income assets can load more heavily on the wedge component. Overall, the framework offers an accessible way to separate opportunity cost from cash-flow forecast distortion within DCF valuation.

title: What Does Ordinary Least Squares Measure? Economic States, Deviations, and the Interpretation of Regression
affiliations: Nguyen Tat Thanh University

detail.title: What Does Ordinary Least Squares Measure? Economic States, Deviations, and the Interpretation of Regression

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: This chapter revisits the historical origins of ordinary least squares to clarify a structural distinction that is often overlooked in modern econometrics. Drawing on the contrast between Legendre's original measurement view and Gauss's later probabilistic reinterpretation, the chapter shows that contemporary regression analysis operates primarily in deviation space rather than at the level of economic quantities. By decomposing variables into state and deviation components, it becomes clear that regression coefficients, intercepts, and residuals have meanings that differ fundamentally from their interpretation as measurements of economic structure. The chapter introduces the concepts of state coefficient, deviation coefficient, state intercept, and adjustment component, and demonstrates how the standard hypothesis 𝑏 = 0 differs from a stateconsistency hypothesis 𝑏 = 𝑏 𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑒. Numerical and algebraic illustrations show situations where econometrics becomes silent while economic meaning remains fully present. The analysis provides the conceptual bridge between the discussion of endogenous causality in Chapter 1 and the interpretation of regression models in subsequent chapters.

title: The Confidence Loop: How AI Narratives and Passive Capital are Reshaping
affiliations: Universidad Anahuac Mexico

detail.title: The Confidence Loop: How AI Narratives and Passive Capital are Reshaping

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with any individuals or organizations that could have influenced the research presented in this paper.

detail.abstract: Financial markets have historically priced risk through observable variables such as leverage, credit quality, liquidity conditions, and macroeconomic imbalances. This paper argues that an increasing share of modern systemic risk no longer originates primarily from balance sheets or credit cycles, but from a self-reinforcing confidence loop driven by narrative dominance, passive capital allocation, and derivative-based market structures. In recent years, technological narratives-particularly those surrounding artificial intelligence and long-term productivity transformation-have contributed to an environment in which confidence itself becomes a structural input to market pricing. Passive investment flows, volatility-targeting strategies, and derivative overlays mechanically reinforce price momentum while suppress traditional signals of risk. As a result, markets may display persistent stability precisely at moments when underlying fragility is increasing. This paper proposes a conceptual framework to describe this phenomenon, distinguishing it from both the credit-driven systemic failures of 2008 and earlier speculative episodes. Rather than predicting an imminent crisis, the analysis highlights a structural shift in how risk propagates through modern financial systems and argues for the monitoring of confidence-driven feedback mechanisms as a distinct category of systemic vulnerability.

title: Enhancing Flood Impact Assessment Accuracy: A Comparison of IRIO-Flood Predictions Using HAZUS- and Insurance Claims-Based Business Interruption Estimates
affiliations: Institute of Advanced Study (IUSS - Pavia), University of Pavia - Faculty of Economics, Institute of Advanced Study (IUSS - Pavia), IUSS and IUSS

detail.title: Enhancing Flood Impact Assessment Accuracy: A Comparison of IRIO-Flood Predictions Using HAZUS- and Insurance Claims-Based Business Interruption Estimates
detail.abstract: While input-output models are widely used to assess the economic impacts of natural disasters, their results strongly depend on how disaster shocks are specified. This paper examines two alternative characterizations of flood-induced business interruptions, and their effect on total economic losses. We compare restoration time estimates derived from the Hazus-Flood framework with a novel approach based on micro-level insurance claims data, which allows for partial reductions in plants' productive capacity during the restoration phase, rather than assuming full inoperability. Using georeferenced plant-level data and high-resolution flood maps, we calibrate flood shocks for four major Italian flood events and simulate their propagation through the economy using the IRIO-Flood model. We find that Hazus-based specifications generally produce larger and more dispersed estimates of productive capacity contractions, leading to greater GDP and sectoral output losses-particularly in the short term-and to stronger spillovers to regions not directly affected by the flood. Despite these substantial differences in magnitude, both approaches identify broadly similar patterns in terms of the most affected sectors and regions, with discrepancies emerging more frequently when considering the medium-term propagation of losses. These results highlight the importance of accurate shock specification and suggest that the two proposed methods can be viewed as complementary tools for flood impact and risk assessment.

title: A Comparative Analysis of Some Aspects of Economic Policy in Hungary and Romania
affiliations: MGIMO

detail.title: A Comparative Analysis of Some Aspects of Economic Policy in Hungary and Romania
detail.abstract: The objective of this study is to examine the factors that have enabled Romania to surpass many of Hungary's macroeconomic indicators while maintaining Hungary's advantage in social development indicators. The study's hypothesis assumes that the current set of macroeconomic indicators in a given country is determined by several factors, with a primary focus on the content and nature of economic policy. An examination of the components of economic policy in Hungary and Romania revealed similarities in the instruments used and the officially formulated economic policy goals. The resource base of both countries, considered a constraint on the effectiveness of economic policy, is characterized by increasing depletion overall, but differs in the types of resources in each country. It is concluded that one of the significant reasons for Romania's improved economic indicators at the macro level in recent years has been the consistent implementation of neoliberal recommendations, which, compared to Hungary, have ensured positive macroeconomic performance but have failed to achieve a more socially equitable redistribution of gross domestic product.

title: Firm-Level Exposure to Geopolitical Risk and Corporate Investment
affiliations: Lincoln University (NZ), Lincoln University and Universitas Indonesia

detail.title: Firm-Level Exposure to Geopolitical Risk and Corporate Investment
detail.abstract: We propose novel measurements of firm-level geopolitical risk exposure via textual analysis of 10-K filings of US firms. By leveraging firms' forward-looking and backward-looking disclosures, we distinguish between ex-ante and ex-post geopolitical risk exposure. Our empirical results suggest that firms increase investment in response to higher ex-ante risk exposure, supporting the convexity mechanism of uncertainty on investment. Conversely, firms reduce investment when facing higher ex-post risk, lending support for the real option effect widely documented in the literature. We posit that the effect of geopolitical risk on investment is asymmetric and depends on whether geopolitical risk exposure is materialized. Collectively, both facets of geopolitical risk exposure oppositely predict investment, noting that the explained variation and predictive power are significantly stronger at the investment tails compared to the macro-level geopolitical risk index's. Further analysis show that the effect of ex-ante risk manifests in competition, but it is not the case for ex-post risk.

title: Language as a Coordination Stress Test
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Language as a Coordination Stress Test
detail.abstract: Language is commonly treated as a semantic problem: when coordination fails, the assumed cause is ambiguity, imprecision, or misunderstanding of definitions. This paper proposes a different diagnosis. It examines language as a coordination medium and argues that many persistent failures arise not from unclear meanings, but from unconditioned interpretive variance across observers. Using a series of minimal case studies, the paper demonstrates how words can function descriptively while failing to coordinate shared understanding, even when definitions, information, and incentives are aligned. The analysis reframes disagreement as a structural phenomenon rather than a moral or communicative deficit, and treats failed alignment as a diagnostic signal rather than an error to be corrected. The paper is intentionally written as a stress test: if its diagnosis is correct, independent analytical readers should converge on the same failure mode without relying on shared premises or prescriptive solutions.

title: Bounded Rationality, Societal Progress, Inclusive Institutions: Sustainability and Satisficing Choice
affiliations: University of Perugia

detail.title: Bounded Rationality, Societal Progress, Inclusive Institutions: Sustainability and Satisficing Choice
detail.abstract: Globalization and market-oriented policies have elevated metrics of efficiency, such as income level and profit maximization, to the status of primary indicators of societal progress. However, these maximization rules often misrepresent decision processes that are bounded, multi-attribute, and sensitive to long-term environmental limits. This paper represents an attempt to establish a basic framework – and an expanded one via agent-based model (ABM) – for satisficing choice that integrates agents’ aspiration thresholds and institutional constraints, showing that satisficing equilibria – stable outcomes where agents reach predefined aspiration thresholds – exist under certain conditions and can systematically differ from classical maximizing equilibria. A two-agent model was tested with different optimizers. Propositions that can steer societies toward socially desirable satisficing outcomes were illustrated. The proposed satisficing framework and its resulting policy implications are valuable for economists and policymakers who strive to understand and guide societal progress within environmental and societal constraints.

title: Modelling Exchange Rate Volatility in Kenya: The Role of Monetary Policy
affiliations: University of Eldoret

detail.title: Modelling Exchange Rate Volatility in Kenya: The Role of Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: This research investigates the influence of monetary policy on exchange rate volatility in Kenya, utilizing an annual time series dataset spanning from 1970 to 2024. The study employs the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) model and the Error Correction Model (ECM) to evaluate both long-run and short-run relationships. Exchange rate volatility is assessed using the Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH) model, revealing that past volatility influences current rates. The F-bound test indicates a long-term relationship among the variables. In the long run, exchange rate volatility is affected by interest rates, money supply, and inflation rates. In the short run, it is significantly influenced by its past values, inflation rates, interest rates, and money supply. Managing these factors is crucial for controlling exchange rate fluctuations in Kenya. The findings highlight the need for a stable inflation rate, prudent monetary expansion, and effective interest rate management as key strategies for stabilizing exchange rates. Therefore the study recommends the need for a stable inflation rate, prudent monetary expansion, and effective interest rate management policies as key strategies for stabilizing exchange rates.

title: The State Drift Problem Language, Interpretation, and Coordination
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The State Drift Problem Language, Interpretation, and Coordination
detail.abstract: Every experienced user of frontier AI has encountered the same anomaly: identical prompts, identical documents, identical tasks-yet radically different outcomes. One run produces a concise administrative verdict; another devolves into unsolicited rewrites, pedagogy, or defensive justification. Common explanations-prompt quality, hallucination, misalignment, or reasoning limits-fail to account for the consistency and persistence of this variance.

title: The Benchmark Illusion: Why Current AI Evaluations Cannot Detect Structural Confabulation
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Benchmark Illusion: Why Current AI Evaluations Cannot Detect Structural Confabulation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A - Does not apply as I'm an independent.
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A - No patients or participants involved.
declarations.funderStatement: I founded my own research.

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence benchmarks are presented as evidence of capability, safety and progress. This paper demonstrates that they are structurally incapable of detecting the failures that matter. Current evaluation methodologies measure pattern-matching performance within training distributions while remaining categorically blind to the absence of verification capability. Verification is used here in the strict epistemic sense: the architectural authority of a system to categorically halt or refuse output under conditions of irreducible ignorance, rather than merely producing calibrated uncertainty, internal consistency or evidence-conditioned continuation. This is not a failure of measurement optimisation, but a prior condition: benchmarks cannot measure verification where no verification capability exists, even when evaluation is delegated to more advanced AI models.

Analysis of major evaluation frameworks (including MMLU [18], GSM8K [19], HumanEval [20], HellaSwag [21] and TruthfulQA [22]) reveals a systematic conflation of statistical correlation with understanding. More critically, optimisation against these benchmarks actively amplifies the failure modes documented in Artificially Confabulating and Untrustworthy (ACU) systems [24]: benchmark gaming rewards confident completion over epistemic restraint, fluent articulation over verified accuracy and sophisticated pattern exploitation over genuine reasoning.

The result is an evaluation paradigm that makes unsafe systems appear safe. High benchmark scores correlate with increased confabulation confidence, not reduced confabulation frequency. This finding has immediate regulatory implications: frameworks that reference benchmark performance as safety evidence institutionalise precisely the wrong incentive structure. No evaluation methodology operating within the current paradigm can measure trustworthiness. Trustworthiness requires verification capability (V), which transformer-based architectures structurally lack [24]. The benchmark crisis is therefore conceptual, not technical. Its resolution requires governance frameworks that assume V = 0 and mandate external verification, not better tests administered to systems incapable of the capability being tested.

This paper establishes that no benchmark supplying ground truth can, even in principle, measure verification capability, rendering evaluation-based assurance logically invalid rather than merely empirically unreliable.

Paper One established the architectural diagnosis (V = 0). This paper demonstrates why that diagnosis cannot be detected by current measurement paradigms. Paper Three codifies the governance requirements that follow. Papers Four and Five translate this measurement impossibility into institutional liability and market mispricing.

title: Artificial Confabulation and Untrustworthiness: The Structural Limits of Transformer-Based, Next-Token AI Architectures
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Artificial Confabulation and Untrustworthiness: The Structural Limits of Transformer-Based, Next-Token AI Architectures

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A. I'm independent of organisations and other people, including financial relationships.

detail.abstract:
This is the first paper in a five-part series examining the structural limits, institutional consequences and economic mispricings of contemporary artificial intelligence.

Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) are structurally incapable of verification, defined here as architectural veto authority to halt or refuse output under conditions of irreducible ignorance (V), a core component of epistemic integrity. This paper argues that the architectural absence of V, coupled with the absence of consequence-bearing Experience (E), renders LLMs fundamentally untrustworthy, regardless of scale and performance on pattern-matching benchmarks. This incapacity also prevents organisations from sustaining Sovereign Intelligence: the ability to verify, override and remain accountable for decisions made with or by AI systems.

While most research treats "hallucinations" as behavioural glitches to be solved, the KEV constraint (Knowledge is massive, Experience is absent, Verification is absent) dictates that scaling only intensifies the failure mode, which is taxonomically classified as Artificially Confabulating and Untrustworthy (ACU). This confabulation is not a defect but the architecture operating as designed: fluent completion without truth. This claim concerns model-internal epistemic capacity: tool use, retrieval and external artefacts can support system-level checking, but they do not create internal verification capability and therefore cannot be treated as self-verification.

The paper draws a parallel with clinical confabulation, documents the compounding failure stack (Speed-Weighted Reasoning Collapse → Architectural Confabulation → Uncalibrated Confidence) and presents systematic adversarial interrogation across frontier systems to demonstrate cross-model repeatability. Ensembling, debate and multi-agent coordination may reduce error rates in some tasks; however, agreement among generators is not evidence of truth and does not resolve the absence of verification (V = 0).

The path forward is not autonomous AI but Governed Hybrid Intelligence (GHI): human judgement augmented by machine synthesis, constrained by external verification that supplies the grounding the architecture lacks. Without GHI, scaling produces more sophisticated confabulation, not more reliable intelligence.

This paper establishes the diagnostic foundation. Papers Two and Three complete the architectural analysis. Papers Four and Five translate this diagnosis into institutional liability and market mispricing. What is established here is not merely theoretical. It creates consequences.

title: The Work of UNCITRAL Working Group III: How Process Shapes Outcomes
affiliations: University of New South Wales (UNSW) and CNRS

detail.title: The Work of UNCITRAL Working Group III: How Process Shapes Outcomes

keywords: United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL)

publicationDetails.detailsText: In Bonnitcha & Titi (eds), ISDS Reform: Past, Present, and Future, Special Issue: JWIT (2026)

detail.abstract: This article seeks to trace how the multilateral processes of deliberation, debate, and decision-making within the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL) shape the outcomes that are emerging from the negotiations on reform of investor-State dispute settlement (ISDS) in Working Group III. The article explores how the Working Group came to receive its mandate and how that mandate was defined, before turning to its working methods. After identifying key junctures and decision-making points in the eight years of negotiations, highlighting how the Working Group's methods and procedures have influenced the framing and resolution of contentious issues, the article reviews the status of each of the current 'reform elements' under development. This is also an opportunity to consider the way in which issues have been grouped together and what has slipped off the agenda. A final section introduces the other contributions to the Special Issue.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Large Language Model Collaboration
affiliations: Imperial College London - Department of Computing, Imperial College London - Department of Computing and Imperial College London - Department of Computing

detail.title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Large Language Model Collaboration
detail.abstract: This study investigates cooperative LLM collaboration through a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework, where agents are jointly optimized using a shared group reward rather than independent objectives. A multi-agent GRPO (MAGRPO) algorithm is proposed to stabilize learning under decentralized execution. Evaluation is performed on 4 collaborative benchmarks covering reasoning, writing, and code synthesis, totaling 5,200 training episodes. Results show that MAGRPO improves average task reward by 27.6%, reduces inter-agent contradiction rates by 31.2%, and accelerates convergence by 1.8× compared to independent RL fine-tuning.

title: Multi-Agent Post-Co-Training of Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
affiliations: Princeton University - Department of Computer Science, Princeton University - Department of Computer Science and Princeton University - Department of Computer Science

detail.title: Multi-Agent Post-Co-Training of Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
detail.abstract: This study introduces MAPoRL2, a post-training framework that enhances collaborative LLM performance through multi-agent reinforcement learning and structured discussion. Multiple LLM agents independently generate candidate solutions, engage in iterative discussion rounds, and are jointly optimized using verifier-based rewards that assess both correctness and corrective reasoning. Experiments across 5 reasoning and generation benchmarks with 4,500 training samples demonstrate improvements of 18.9% in answer accuracy and 22.4% in correction efficiency over single-agent post-training, highlighting the effectiveness of discussion-aware RL signals.

detail.abstract: In an era characterized by rapid technological change, intense competition, and evolving consumer expectations, organizations must continuously innovate to remain relevant. Traditional innovation models are increasingly inadequate to address complex and uncertain business problems. In this context, design thinking and crowdsourcing have emerged as powerful tools that enable organizations to foster innovation and cultivate an entrepreneurial mindset. This article explores the conceptual foundations of design thinking and crowdsourcing, examines their complementary roles in the innovation process, and explains how their integration promotes creativity, opportunity recognition, and entrepreneurial behaviour in modern organizations.

title: Nineteenth-Century Navigable Waters
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University - Penn State Dickinson Law

detail.title: Nineteenth-Century Navigable Waters
detail.abstract: The Supreme Court's doctrinal Odyssey with "navigable waters" began in the nineteenth century and spanned a tremendous range of constitutional and statutory disputes. Indeed, by century's end, the Court had taken more opportunities to opine on what comprised "navigable waters" than perhaps any other doctrinal term. The Court's misadventures with the term continued in the twentieth century, but those contests were shaped in largest part by the confusing cross currents churned up from the nineteenth. Today, as the Court so regularly acts by doctrinal fiat, this history should be under a great deal more scrutiny than it has been in a long time. What it reveals, beyond considerable judicial conceit, is the treachery inherent in judges deciding for the republic what our real interests in these waters are and why and how they should be governed.

title: The Interrelationship between Organizational Climate, Employee Performance, and Competitive Advantage
affiliations: Walden University

detail.title: The Interrelationship between Organizational Climate, Employee Performance, and Competitive Advantage
detail.abstract: As we approach 2026, organizations are navigating an environment marked by significant changes that are fundamentally transforming traditional practices and management paradigms. This research suggests that organizations that actively create a climate supportive of employee engagement, professional growth, and overall wellbeing are more likely to improve performance, foster innovation aligned with market demands, and ultimately gain a sustainable competitive advantage. The primary objective of this study is to investigate the relationship between two crucial organizational variables: organizational climate and employee performance, to understand how they contribute to achieving competitive advantage for firms. To address the research questions and test the relevant hypotheses, a quantitative approach will be utilized, implementing various statistical techniques. A thorough review of the literature reveals a clear gap in understanding the relationships among organizational climate, employee performance, and competitive advantage, with scholars offering differing views on these connections. The expected outcomes of this study will help deepen understanding of these dynamics and their influence on organizational effectiveness in today's business environment. This study makes a significant contribution to understanding the relationships between research variables at both the applied and theoretical levels. The model developed in the study enables organizations to identify the optimal point at which enhancing the organizational climate yields a competitive advantage, underscoring the importance of human capital. This contribution serves as a foundation for future research and practical recommendations for managers in the organizational field.

title: Voluntary Agreements in Environmental Policy: A Narrative Review of Design Logics, Behavioral Mechanisms, and Institutional Conditions

detail.title: Voluntary Agreements in Environmental Policy: A Narrative Review of Design Logics, Behavioral Mechanisms, and Institutional Conditions
detail.abstract: Environmental Voluntary Agreements (VAs) have been widely adopted as flexible policy instruments intended to complement-or, at times, substitute-traditional command-and-control regulation. This narrative review synthesizes multidisciplinary scholarship on VAs with three aims: (1) to consolidate core definitions and typologies used across environmental economics and public policy; (2) to organize the literature around the key mechanisms through which VAs are expected to produce environmental improvements (efficiency, reputational incentives, credible regulatory threat, and learning); and (3) to assess how institutional capacity, implementation dynamics, and behavioral policy concepts (choice architecture/nudging) condition VA performance. Drawing on foundational and applied work.

title: Taxes and Competition: Evidence from the Airline Industry
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management and Boston University - Questrom School of Business

detail.title: Taxes and Competition: Evidence from the Airline Industry

publicationDetails.detailsText: MIT Sloan Research Paper (forthcoming)
publicationDetails.journalName: MIT Sloan School of Management Working Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Accounting & Economics, forthcoming

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether corporate tax cuts alter product-market competition by differentially affecting firms with high versus low tax burdens. Tax cuts increase after-tax cash flows for profitable firms but provide little immediate benefit to loss-making firms. We study the 1986 Tax Reform Act, which reduced the top corporate tax rate by 12 percentage points and examine route-level price and quantity data from the U.S. airline industry. We find that, in response to the Act, profitable airlines reduce ticket prices by 4.2% relative to their loss-making rivals and gain 3.3 percentage points in market share. These effects are concentrated in routes where loss-making competitors are financially constrained and are accompanied by increased entry by profitable airlines and exit by loss-making airlines. The evidence suggests that taxes can affect competitive outcomes, specifically in our paper by enabling high-tax firms to compete more aggressively with low-tax rivals after tax cuts.

title: Gamesmanship in Civil Litigation
affiliations: Temple University James E. Beasley School of Law

detail.title: Gamesmanship in Civil Litigation

publicationDetails.detailsText: 60 Georgia L. Rev. 1 (2026)

detail.abstract:
In civil litigation, strategy is everywhere. Some of it is explicitly envisioned by rules of procedure, but other forms of strategy rely more on clever exploitation of gaps in the rules, sometimes through trickery, surprise, or psychological mind games. The role strategy plays in civil litigation is underexamined, which raises two concerns: first, this lack of attention entrenches strategy by default as a procedural value in competition with accuracy, efficiency, and other procedural values. Second, it amplifies the disadvantages experienced by unrepresented litigants. This Article builds on earlier work to examine how courts shape the space that litigants have for strategic behavior, in service of an inquiry into how that space ought to be shaped.

Battles over the meaning and rightful place of strategy in civil litigation tend to play out in the arena of “gamesmanship,” a term courts use with increasing frequency to refer to behavior in the gray zone between the clearly allowed and the clearly disallowed. Strategic behavior in this realm is often unregulated by rules, only weakly governed by norms, and subject to significant judicial discretion. Judicial decisions in cases involving gamesmanship frequently expose tensions between respect for zealous advocacy and concerns about fairness and accuracy.

This Article makes two contributions to our understanding of the role of strategic behavior in civil litigation. First, it examines the meaning of “gamesmanship” in a litigation context and proposes a categorization of gamesmanlike litigation behavior. Second, it applies this categorization in describing how courts use the term “gamesmanship” and surveys and theorizes how they treat behavior they have thus labeled. I argue that the concept functions as three distinct analytical tools: (1) as an aspect of purposive statutory analysis; (2) as a canon of construction; and (3) as an implied mental-state element. The Article concludes by imagining a different approach, more deliberate in delineating the role of “strategy space” in civil litigation and cognizant of the concerns that gamesmanlike behavior can raise.

title: Mass and Digital Media as Agents in the Formation of Political Consciousness
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Mass and Digital Media as Agents in the Formation of Political Consciousness
detail.abstract: This theoretical research article examines the role of mass and digital media in the formation of political consciousness, with particular attention to the process of humanizing political communication in contemporary media environments. Drawing on classical theories of media influence and modern approaches to digital communication, the article argues that media do not merely transmit political information but actively construct political reality through narratives, emotional framing, and personalization. Political consciousness is conceptualized as a socially embedded, culturally mediated, and emotionally structured phenomenon that develops through continuous interaction with mediated representations of politics. The study highlights how digital media intensify these processes by personalizing information flows and integrating politics into everyday communication. The article contributes to ongoing debates on media power, political socialization, and democratic communication by offering a comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding the qualitative dimensions of media influence.

title: The Cost of Clean Transition: Extreme Temperatures, Air Pollution, and Household Energy Poverty
affiliations: Shanghai University, Shanghai University and Shanghai University of International Business and Economics

detail.title: The Cost of Clean Transition: Extreme Temperatures, Air Pollution, and Household Energy Poverty

publicationDetails.detailsText: ENEECO-D-26-00319

detail.abstract: The concurrent pressures of extreme temperatures and air pollution are driving two critical trends: rising household energy demand and an accelerating transition to low-carbon energy. Both trends increase energy expenditures, elevating the risk of energy poverty. To analyze the combined impact and underlying mechanisms of these interrelated factors, we develop an integrated "extreme temperatures–air pollution–energy transition" analytical framework and empirically examine this issue by leveraging China’s Clean Heating policy as a quasi-natural experiment. Our findings reveal that both extreme temperatures and air pollution significantly exacerbate household energy poverty. Given China’s current fossil fuel-dominated energy structure, heightened consumption to cope with extreme temperatures may further worsen air pollution. While the Clean Heating Policy successfully improved local air quality, it concurrently increased energy costs, thereby deepening energy poverty for affected households. These results underscore that advancing energy transition policies requires careful consideration of energy affordability, ensuring that climate and air quality objectives do not impose disproportionate burdens on vulnerable populations.

title: Where Geopolitical Risk Binds: Stockpiling and AI as Complementary Strategies for Mitigating Supply Chain Risk in Critical Minerals
affiliations: University of Tasmania - School of Economics and Finance, Monash University - Department of Economics,  and Monash Business School

detail.title: Where Geopolitical Risk Binds: Stockpiling and AI as Complementary Strategies for Mitigating Supply Chain Risk in Critical Minerals

publicationDetails.detailsText: ENEECO-D-26-00386

detail.abstract: We develop novel, stage-specific, geopolitical risk indicators to examine how geopolitical risk is distributed across the supply-chain for lithium and copper, two minerals which are vital for low-carbon technologies. We find that refining is the geopolitical bottleneck for both minerals, reflecting that refining capacity is highly concentrated in China. We examine refining diversification, strategic stockpiling, and AI-driven productivity gains as complementary policy instruments for mitigating exposure to geopolitical risk at the refining stage. We show that reducing China’s refining share substantially lowers refining-stage geopolitical risk, with larger gains for lithium than for copper. We find that stockpiling plays a critical role in buffering near-term geopolitical shocks, but significantly increases the projected shortfall in copper and lithium which is needed to realize the clean energy transition under alternative Net Zero pathways. We demonstrate that AI-driven productivity gains will be needed to narrow the projected supply gaps for both minerals. Our results suggest that ensuring effective security of critical minerals requires a coordinated policy mix, combining refining diversification, strategic stockpiling, and productivity-enhancing technological change.

title: Why AI Economics Fail: Cost Structures, Billing Models, and Stalled Adoption
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Why AI Economics Fail: Cost Structures, Billing Models, and Stalled Adoption
detail.abstract: Despite rapid advances in model capability, large-scale adoption of generative artificial intelligence has stalled. This paper argues that the constraint is not technical performance but economic viability and user trust. On the supply side, current AI business models rely on pricing proxies-tokens and flat-rate subscriptions-that fail to reflect underlying compute costs or user value, leading to uncontrolled operating expenses and weak revenue alignment. On the demand side, adoption has plateaued because users do not trust systems that lack reliable memory and consistent, user-controlled behavior. Using publicly available disclosures, earnings call statements, and observable usage patterns, this paper presents a bounded, testable claim: absent fundamental changes to cost provisioning, billing, memory persistence, and governance, AI systems cannot scale profitably or achieve durable enterprise adoption. The paper concludes by outlining observable implications and explicitly inviting rebuttal.

title: Can Blockchain Improve Gains from Trade in Markets?
affiliations: Macquarie University and Macquarie University, Macquarie Business School

detail.title: Can Blockchain Improve Gains from Trade in Markets?
detail.abstract: We quantify the impact of alternative settlement architectures on gains from trade in financial markets. We model permissionless and permissioned blockchain settlement systems in which block size and block time are chosen to maximize gains from trade subject to a no-settlement-failure constraint, trading off settlement speed and transaction fees against settlement integrity. Calibrating the model to multiple markets, we find that permissionless blockchains are optimal in markets with high trading volume and small trade sizes, such as US equities, while permissioned blockchains are optimal in markets with larger trades, such as corporate bonds, Treasury bills, and gold. Relative to legacy systems, optimal settlement design increases gains from trade by 9-39 percent across markets, with aggregate gains on the order of $40 billion per year.

title: Recurrent Severe Weather Events and Herders' Livelihood: Evidence from Mongolia
affiliations: , National University of Mongolia - Economic Research Institute,  and

detail.title: Recurrent Severe Weather Events and Herders' Livelihood: Evidence from Mongolia

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All authors have no competing interests to declare.

detail.abstract: Dzud, a harsh winter and spring event that leads to high livestock mortality, has become increasingly recurrent in Mongolia due to climate change, causing substantial damage despite ongoing adaptation and mitigation efforts. This study analyzes the impacts of dzud on rural herder household livelihoods across Mongolia by utilizing a constructed province-level panel dataset from 2009 to 2023. The effects are estimated using a two-way fixed effects regression with an instrumental variable to account for potential endogeneity of migration. We find three main results. First, dzud events have an immediate and adverse effect on rural herder household real income and expenditure, with livestock income particularly vulnerable. Second, when heterogeneity is considered, middle-income households are affected the most, and households headed by individuals under the age of 35 experience larger income declines compared to those headed by older individuals. Third, dzud events' impact on income inequality for herder households is not significant since its estimate is not robust. These findings underscore the differential vulnerability of herders to climatic shocks and highlight the need for policies that mitigate the economic consequences of such extreme events.

title: Automation, Artificial Intelligence, and Employment in the European Union: An Early-Stage Meta-Analysis of Macroeconomic Evidence
affiliations: , Kozminski University, Kozminski University and Kozminski University

detail.title: Automation, Artificial Intelligence, and Employment in the European Union: An Early-Stage Meta-Analysis of Macroeconomic Evidence

declarations.funderStatement: This research has received funding from the European Union’s Horizon Europe research and innovation program under grant agreement No 101132476 (Link4Skills project).

detail.abstract: This paper provides a meta-analysis of macroeconomic, quantitative studies that seek to identify the causal impact of automation and artificial intelligence (AI) on employment in the European Union (EU). We contribute an EU-focused synthesis that concentrates on macro-level evidence, complementing a literature dominated by micro task-based analyses and broader cross-country discussions. Using an AI-assisted workflow for search, screening, and extraction with human oversight, we map the available evidence and report clear methodological and knowledge gaps. A central finding is that the automation and robotics literature is comparatively developed, while credible causal macro evidence on AI itself remains sparse and fragmented. We treat this scarcity as a result that motivates a concrete research agenda. Across the core empirical studies and selected grey literature, the net employment effect appears modestly positive on the order of 1.5 to 2.0 percent, but the distributional pattern is uneven. Risks concentrate among low-skilled and routine workers, older cohorts, and lagging regions, pointing to policy priorities in reskilling, education, and digital infrastructure. Methodologically, the paper demonstrates how LLM-assisted procedures can improve transparency, consistency, and scalability in early-stage evidence synthesis where conventional meta-regression is premature.

title: A Homegrown Anti-Poverty Toolkit: Mixed-Methods Evaluation of a Community- Led, Multi-Sectoral Development Program for Historically- Known “Batwa” in Rwanda 2008-2025

detail.abstract:
Background: Most Rwandans historically known as “Batwa” experience high infant mortality and low life expectancy, with significant marginalization and poverty. Evidence is lacking for interventions yielding sustainable development outcomes.

Methods: We conducted a longitudinal mixed-methods evaluation of the Community of Potters’ Health and Development (COPHAD) program, initiated in 2008 in the forest settlement of Bwiza and continued through 2025 in Cyaruzinge because of government - mandated relocation.We obtained quantitative data through population-based household surveys adapted from the Rwanda Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) in 2009, 2011, and 2024; with DHS’ national poorest-quintile benchmarks as a control.We obtained qualitative data through videotaped semi-structured interviews (2011–2024), analyzed using thematic analysis with iterative coding. We triangulated data through structured focus group assessments in 2023. We produced, applied and refined a “homegrown” anti-poverty toolkit through iterative implementation and evaluation.

Findings: Over three years, we documented statistically significant advances in 12 measures of food security, access to healthcare, sanitation, hygiene and jobs; elimination of Kwashiorkor; and emergence of women leaders. Over sixteen years, we documented: increased child survival; “solving malnutrition; improving health; hygiene; education; family planning; and living standards.” Estimated daily per-capita income increased from approximately US$0·01 at baseline to US$0·44 by 2024.

Interpretation: A co-created, culturally grounded, multi-sectoral development strategy, implemented with long-term accompaniment, can promote sustained improvements in health, economy, and social integration for forest-dwelling, and relocated “Batwa”. Further research is needed to assess scalability, cost-effectiveness, and transferability to other settings.

title: Streamlining Financial Audits and Compliance Through Data Pipeline Automation in Multi-Sector Organisations
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Streamlining Financial Audits and Compliance Through Data Pipeline Automation in Multi-Sector Organisations
detail.abstract:
In many organisations, the audit does not begin when the auditors arrive. It begins months earlier, quietly and painfully, as finance teams start reconstructing trails that should already exist. Spreadsheets are pulled from shared drives. ¹ Emails are searched for approvals that were never logged centrally. Data is reconciled manually across systems that were never designed to speak to one another. By the time the formal audit starts, the organisation is already exhausted. 
This pattern is not confined to one sector. Public agencies, financial institutions, healthcare providers, manufacturing firms, and NGOs all face the same underlying problem: compliance has grown more complex, while the systems that support it remain fragmented. Regulatory expectations now demand continuous assurance rather than periodic reporting, yet many organisations still operate as though audits are rare events rather than an ever-present obligation¹.
Data pipeline automation is emerging as a structural response to this mismatch. Rather than treating audits as episodic exercises in reconstruction, automated data pipelines embed compliance into everyday operations. Financial data is captured, validated, transformed, and logged as it moves through the organisation, creating an audit-ready environment by default rather than by emergency effort. ² 
This article examines how data pipeline automation can fundamentally reshape financial audits and compliance in multi-sector organisations. It focuses not only on technology, but on process design, governance, human behaviour, and the trade-offs that leaders must navigate to make automation credible, ethical, and effective.

title: Towards a Foundation for Intelligent Contracts
affiliations: Leiden University, Independent, Independent, Leiden University - Leiden Law School, Leiden University - Center for Law and Digital Technologies, Independent and Independent

detail.title: Towards a Foundation for Intelligent Contracts

publicationDetails.detailsText: 15th International Conference on Agents and Artificial Intelligence (ICAART 2023), Volume 2, Pp. 87-98

detail.abstract: This article investigates the incorporation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) within LegalTech. We define an ontology to form the basis for Trustworthy AI processing of contract automation. The value of our research is that it applies an ontology, as existing tool, in contract automation. Two perspectives are emphasized: communications analysis and risk analysis. They are explored under a new prism. Our context is Intelligent Contracts (iContracts), which aim at reducing the time-consuming and often complex contractual process by minimizing human involvement. Contract communications and risk analysis processes are often neglected in automation. Therefore, our research investigates to what extent is possible to design an ontology for contract automation based upon the combination of both. Our methodology is twofolded. First, we concentrate on applying key word search on an online database to demonstrate the lack of available solutions. Second, we develop an ontology based upon a case study of a freelancer agreement. Of course, we use existing literature to further engineer the ontology. Our finding shows that 9.4 percent of LegalTech solutions deal with contract automation. From them, 0.7 percent focus on communications and risk automation for contracting. The conceptual expressiveness of the ontology is validated with research to the use case. A follow-up discussion suggests that the ontology should be further engineered from a third perspective, trustworthiness, and should be re-validated experimentally. Our conclusion underlines the need for further innovation in contract automation, especially in relation to communications and risk data. a

title: PEARL: Prototype-Enhanced Alignment for Label-Efficient Representation Learning with Deployment-Driven Insights from Digital Governance Communication Systems
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong - Department of Politics and Public Administration, Hong Kong Polytechnic University - Department of Applied Social Sciences, The University of Hong Kong - Department of Politics and Public Administration, Lanzhou University and Hong Kong Polytechnic University

detail.title: PEARL: Prototype-Enhanced Alignment for Label-Efficient Representation Learning with Deployment-Driven Insights from Digital Governance Communication Systems
detail.abstract: In many deployed systems, new text inputs are handled by retrieving similar past cases-for example, routing and responding to citizen messages in digital governance platforms. When these systems fail, the issue is often not the language model itself, but that the nearest neighbors in the embedding space correspond to the wrong cases. Modern machine learning systems increasingly rely on fixed, highdimensional embeddings produced by large pretrained models and sentence encoders. In real-world deployments, labels are scarce, domains shift over time, and retraining the base encoder is expensive or infeasible. As a result, downstream performance depends heavily on embedding geometry. Yet raw embeddings are often poorly aligned with the local neighborhood structure required by nearest-neighbor retrieval, similarity search, and lightweight classifiers that operate directly on embeddings. We propose PEARL (Prototype-Enhanced Aligned Representation Learning), a labelefficient approach that uses limited supervision to softly align embeddings toward class prototypes. The method reshapes local neighborhood geometry while preserving dimensionality and avoiding aggressive projection or collapse. Its aim is to bridge the gap between purely unsupervised postprocessing, which offers limited and inconsistent gains, and fully supervised projections that require substantial labeled data. We evaluate PEARL under controlled label regimes ranging from extreme label scarcity to higher-label settings. In the label-scarce condition, PEARL substantially improves local neighborhood quality, yielding 25.7% gains over raw embeddings and over 21.1% gains relative to strong unsupervised post-processing, precisely in the regime where similarity-based systems are most brittle. As label availability increases, fully supervised projections can achieve stronger performance on some tasks, while PEARL remains a robust and practical preprocessing step that delivers reliable improvements with minimal supervision.

title: Preparing for the Next Round of New gTLDs: Governance and Resilience Lessons for Applicants

detail.title: Preparing for the Next Round of New gTLDs: Governance and Resilience Lessons for Applicants
detail.abstract: As the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN) prepares to launch a second round of new generic Top-Level Domain (gTLD) applications, applicant preparedness is often framed in narrow technical and financial terms. This paper argues that such an approach is increasingly insufficient. Drawing on governance precedents, objection dynamics, and institutional patterns emerging from the first application round, it identifies non-technical risks that have proven decisive in application outcomes. The analysis introduces three practical frameworks-the Adversary Map, the Precedent Map, and the Resilience Map-to help future applicants assess political exposure, procedural vulnerability, and long-term institutional endurance. It further contends that new gTLD applications should be understood not as short-term compliance exercises, but as multi-year governance engagements requiring sustained executive alignment, legal resilience, and strategic diplomacy. By reframing preparedness as a governance and resilience challenge rather than a checklist exercise, this paper offers forward-looking guidance to organizations seeking to navigate ICANN's next gTLD round with greater strategic awareness and reduced institutional risk.

detail.abstract: We take advantage of recent advances in behavioral genetics to revisit a classic question in economics: how do parents respond to children's endowments and to differences in endowments between siblings? We use a summary index based on DNA, which is fixed at conception and assigned randomly across siblings, as a proxy for educational endowments. We find that parents of non-twins display inequality aversion: given the absolute endowment level of one child, they invest less in him/her if his/her sibling has a lower genetic predisposition to educational attainment. In contrast, we find no evidence that parents of dizygotic twins react to endowment differences between their children.

title: Second-Best Incentive-Compatible Risk Sharing with a Continuum of Agents and General Risk Measures
affiliations: Heriot-Watt University

detail.title: Second-Best Incentive-Compatible Risk Sharing with a Continuum of Agents and General Risk Measures
detail.abstract: This paper examines second-best risk sharing in a continuum economy with private information when agents assess contingent allocations using conditional, law-invariant convex monetary risk measures. The planner is restricted to anonymous, distribution-based mechanisms and must respect an incentive requirement suited to large pools: price-taking Bayesian incentive compatibility, under which each agent treats the aggregate distribution of reports as exogenous. Under standard regularity conditions, including the Fatou property, we establish existence of an optimal incentive-feasible allocation. We then provide a dual characterization of the optimum in the form of a risk-adjusted state-price density together with an incentive wedge. Subgradients of the conditional risk measures act as type-dependent valuation kernels, while incentive constraints introduce state-contingent distortions that modify marginal risk transfers across reports. The characterization nests the classical Borch--Wilson efficiency rule as a special case and links implementability directly to convex-duality objects associated with risk measures. Examples with entropic and Expected-Shortfall/CVaR criteria illustrate how incentive distortions concentrate in tail states and generate deductible-, limit-, and layer-type contract features.

title: Institutional Foundations: A Comparative Analysis of Voluntary Environmental Agreements in Chile and United States of America

detail.title: Institutional Foundations: A Comparative Analysis of Voluntary Environmental Agreements in Chile and United States of America
detail.abstract: This study conducts a comparative institutional analysis of environmental Voluntary Agreements (VAs) in the United States and Clean Production Agreements (APLs) in Chile. While the U.S. programs-Common Sense Initiative, Project XL, and the 33/50 Program-were initially recognized for promoting voluntary corporate environmental commitments, they were ultimately discontinued due to weak institutional support, high transaction costs, and limited regulatory integration. In contrast, Chile's APLs have demonstrated sustained implementation and success, largely due to their integration within the country's economic institutional framework, led by CORFO and the Ministry of Economy. Using a qualitative research design, this study applies Mill's Method of Concordance, Ostrom's Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework, and Path Dependence theory to identify the institutional and governance factors that explain the divergent trajectories of these programs. The findings highlight the critical role of economic institutions in sustaining collaborative governance mechanisms and fostering publicprivate cooperation. This research contributes to the literature on environmental policy instruments by offering insights for policymakers seeking to enhance the design and sustainability of voluntary environmental programs.

detail.abstract: This article seeks to describe the pertinence, coherence, and coordination of public policies on climate change reported by Chile to the United Nations through its Biennial Update Reports. Finally, we will describe some opportunities for improvement in the coordination and coherence of these public policies.

title: The Effect Of Digital Transformation On The Leader Behaviors: An Implementation At Intermediate Goods Industry

detail.abstract: Societies, climate, nature, individuals, and the world have shifted from slow-motion incremental alterations to rapid and radical changes. In this context, this thesis deals with answering two clear and vital questions: Which characteristics create effective business leaders, and how these behaviors are affected by digital transformation. title: AI-Driven Inventory Optimization in Airline Logistics: Enhancing Efficiency, Sustainability, and Operational Performance

detail.title: AI-Driven Inventory Optimization in Airline Logistics: Enhancing Efficiency, Sustainability, and Operational Performance
detail.abstract: This study examines the application of AI-driven predictive analytics to optimize inventory management in airline logistics. The primary research objectives are to evaluate how these advanced techniques reduce spare-part shortages and excesses, enhance operational efficiency, and contribute indirectly to sustainability by lowering waste and energy consumption. Employing a mixed-methods approach, the research synthesizes quantitative performance metrics such as inventory cost reductions ranging from 25% to 40% and inventory level decreases of 20% to 54% with qualitative insights into strategic implementation and stakeholder engagement. Key findings indicate that integrating machine learning algorithms and simulation-based models not only improves inventory turnover and reduces lead times (by approximately 11.5%) but also achieves near-perfect spare parts availability. The study further highlights substantial financial benefits, including significant cost savings and improved working capital, and outlines actionable recommendations for integrating AI into existing ERP/MRO systems. The results contribute to theoretical frameworks in digital transformation and supply chain management, offering practical implications for airline executives and policymakers seeking to drive operational excellence and sustainable practices in the aviation industry.

title: Macroeconomic Implications of a Tax on Banks’ Profits
