detail.abstract: This paper investigates the potential macroeconomic effects of a tax on banks' profits for the Greek economy. To this end, a Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium (DSGE) model is employed, which allows the identification of the main transmission channels through which a tax on bank profits may affect the real economy and the financial sector. We find that such a tax affects the economy primarily via the banking capital channel and the bank funding channel, constraining the supply of credit, reducing the value of banking collateral and potentially leading to a contraction in economic activity. Overall, the findings highlight that a tax on bank profits may generate adverse effects on both the financial sector and the real economy, underscoring the need for careful policy design and evaluation of such a policy measure.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 972
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The Projects of relevant national interest (PRIN) programme is the most widespread instrument through which the Italian Ministry of University and Research (MUR) funds basic research via competitive procedures. This paper estimates the programme’s impact on publications, patenting capacity, career progression and the creation of new businesses, by comparing the performance of researchers funded for the first time by the 2015 and 2017 calls with that of researchers deemed eligible for funding but who were not financed because the funds ran out. The results show that PRIN programmes had a positive impact on the number of publications, including those of high quality. The effect was greater for the 2017 call, which featured more generous funding, and was driven by the STEM, biology and medical sciences fields. Younger researchers, and to some extent women, experienced a much more pronounced positive effect than the average. Patent activity and researchers’ careers were not influenced by PRIN funding, while the effect on new business creation was positive, but only driven by medical fields.

title: Fading Glamour: Are Italy’s Fashion Exports in Trouble?
affiliations: Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: Fading Glamour: Are Italy’s Fashion Exports in Trouble?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 971
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Historically, Italy has been known for its successful fashion industry (textiles, wearing apparel and leather). This article analyses the drivers of the recent downturn in the country’s fashion exports. Over the years 2019-24, Italy’s fashion export share in world markets remained stable, as a result, however, of weakening exports matching sluggish global demand. In 2022-24, the volume of Italy’s fashion exports declined significantly; the fall was broad-based across the three branches and particularly marked for leather goods. Foreign sales for Italy’s top 1 per cent of fashion exporters contracted the most; luxury goods exporters fared worse than ‘fast-fashion’ firms, especially in the leather goods branch. In the short term, demand for Italy’s fashion exports is not expected to strengthen; US tariffs and Chinese export diversion to third markets pose downward risks, despite a possible buffer stemming from the high-quality positioning of Italy’s exports.

title: Spatial Decision Support Systems for Flood, Fire, and Earthquake Management: Integrating GIS, Decision Analytics, and Emergency Response Frameworks

detail.title: Spatial Decision Support Systems for Flood, Fire, and Earthquake Management: Integrating GIS, Decision Analytics, and Emergency Response Frameworks
detail.abstract:
Urban and rural environments are increasingly exposed to multi-hazard risks, including floods, fires, and earthquakes, posing significant challenges to disaster preparedness and response (Rezvani et al.; Rezaei et al.). This study presents a systematic synthesis of spatial decision support system (SDSS) applications across these hazards, integrating GIS-based and decision-analytic frameworks to assess their effectiveness in disaster management (Estelaji et al.; Suarez et al.). The analysis indicates that SDSS enhances situational awareness, accelerates response times, and strengthens resilience planning by providing actionable, spatially explicit information to decision-makers (Designing and Evaluating Interactive Web Maps).
However, the effectiveness of these systems is contingent upon the granularity and quality of available data, institutional capacity, and the level of user training (Measuring the Impact of Targeted GIS Training). Findings suggest that SDSS can serve as a scalable, evidence-driven foundation for multi-hazard management when properly aligned with governance structures, capacity-building initiatives, and robust data infrastructure. For policymakers, these insights highlight the importance of investing in data integration, targeted training programs, and institutional support to maximize SDSS utility. Future research should explore longitudinal and multi-hazard simulations to refine predictive capabilities and optimize system performance under varying operational contexts.

title: Governance of Artificial Intelligence: Public Policy and Self-Regulatory Frameworks for Consequential Decision-Making

detail.title: Governance of Artificial Intelligence: Public Policy and Self-Regulatory Frameworks for Consequential Decision-Making
detail.abstract: Organizations have increasingly relied on artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning algorithms to generate predictions that feed into consequential decision-making. While AI has augmented some functional aspects of organizations, decision makers face challenges and risks when the use of AI technologies affects stakeholder wellbeing such as those pertaining to employee selection, employee performance evaluation, medical recommendation, and insurance claim rejection. Drawing on real-world examples of employment and healthcare decisions, this chapter of the Handbook on Artificial Intelligence and Strategy provides an overview of the promise and the peril of using AI. The chapter highlights the public policy and self-regulatory frameworks governing AI in decision-making and suggests ways that organizations can reap the benefits of AI through not only risk avoidance but also value creation. The overview informs scholars, professionals, and regulators about how AI governance may be designed to improve stakeholder wellbeing and the quality of decision-making at organizations.

title: Climate Risk (Physical and Transition) on Financial Stability: Impact Modeling in Credit and Market Scenarios

detail.abstract: This study examines the systemic impact of climate change on Indonesia's financial stability through physical and transition risk channels. Physical risks, such as extreme weather, are modeled to escalate credit risk by increasing Non-Performing Loan (NPL) ratios due to asset impairment. Simultaneously, transition risks—driven by carbon policies—trigger market volatility and asset devaluation. Integrating Signaling Theory and Financial Distress Theory, this research aligns with the framework of Oktasari et al. (2022), identifying that climate-induced costs erode net profit and cash flow, thereby serving as primary catalysts for corporate insolvency. The findings suggest that implementing Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) and Green Sukuk is essential for mitigating these risks. This paper provides a strategic foundation for regulators and financial institutions to build climate-resilient financial frameworks.

title: Place-Based Industrial Policies and Local Agglomeration in the Long Run

detail.abstract: This paper estimates the long-run effects of place-based industrial policy, studying a program implemented in Italy in the 1960s and 1970s. Leveraging administrative data over a century and exogenous variation in the assignment rules, we document agglomeration of workers and firms in the targeted clusters lasting well beyond the policy’s termination. By promoting high-technology industries, the intervention spurred demand for business services and fostered a skilled local workforce. Over time, this produced spillovers from manufacturing to knowledge-intensive services, with sustained gains in local wages and human capital. We illustrate how these persistent effects depended on the initial conditions of host locations.

title: Shrinkflation as Exploitation: A Two-Speed Model with Consumer Inattention

detail.title: Shrinkflation as Exploitation: A Two-Speed Model with Consumer Inattention

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a theoretical study and does not involve human participants, personal data, or experiments.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: I develop a theoretical framework to study firms' incentives to reduce package size rather than raise nominal prices—a phenomenon known as shrinkflation—in a market with heterogeneous consumer attention to package size. In equilibrium, firms exploit inattention by choosing package sizes below the socially efficient level and extracting an exploitation premium. Unlike models of shrouded attributes, a non-excludability trap arises: even attentive consumers cannot avoid the distortion, since all buyers purchase the same downsized product. Competition mitigates shrinkflation but does not eliminate it, as exploitation persists. While package size increases relative to monopoly, competition amplifies unit-price exploitation when consumers are inattentive. To capture observed adjustment patterns, I introduce menu costs for package size adjustments and embed the model in a dynamic environment with gradually rising production costs. This generates a two-speed adjustment process: prices adjust continuously in response to cost increases, while package sizes adjust discretely when accumulated profit losses exceed a fixed adjustment cost. I show that information-based policies that increase the salience of unit prices reduce the exploitation margin and improve consumer outcomes, regardless of market structure.

title: The Due Diligence Gap: Why AI Capability Claims Cannot Be Verified by Design

detail.title: The Due Diligence Gap: Why AI Capability Claims Cannot Be Verified by Design

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence has attracted unprecedented levels of capital on the assumption that current systems can reliably reason, plan and adjudicate truth under novel conditions. This paper demonstrates that those assumptions are structurally untestable under prevailing due diligence practices, not because diligence is weak, but because the capability being valued is absent from the underlying architecture.

Papers One to Three established that transformer-based systems lack intrinsic verification capability (V = 0) [1], that evaluation methodologies cannot detect this absence and that organisations deploying such systems accumulate epistemic debt as a latent, non-recognised liability [2, 3]. Paper Four demonstrated how this liability manifests institutionally. This paper extends the analysis into capital markets.

The central finding is a category error. Investors are valuing epistemic capability (reasoning, verification and judgement) while acquiring architecture that produces fluent completion without epistemic authority. Technical due diligence, reliant on benchmarks, demonstrations and expert conviction, is structurally incapable of detecting this mismatch. Evaluation substitutes for verification in investor reasoning.

The result is correlated mispricing. Valuations converge because they rest on the same untestable premise. Failure risk is correlated because the same architectural substrate underpins deployment. Liability accumulates invisibly because verification is absent, while insurance markets increasingly refuse to underwrite the exposure [4].

This paper argues neither that AI lacks commercial value nor that investment is irrational. It demonstrates that markets are pricing properties that cannot be verified in principle by the instruments used to assess them. Until verification is explicitly instantiated, valuations necessarily rest on architectural assumption rather than demonstrable capability.

title: Epistemic Debt: The Economics of Ungoverned AI
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Epistemic Debt: The Economics of Ungoverned AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A - None.
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/a - No participants involved.

detail.abstract:
Ungoverned AI systems that lack verification capability create uninsurable structural liability. They do not fail randomly. They systematically convert epistemic risk into financial, legal and institutional liability.

This condition is not inherent to AI use: governed deployment restores attribution, bounds liability and re-establishes insurability by reinstating external verification authority.

This paper introduces Epistemic Debt as a balance-sheet construct: the accumulated liability incurred when consequential decisions are made without verification while organisational verification capacity simultaneously erodes. Unlike technical debt, epistemic debt compounds silently, becomes visible only at the point of failure and may be irrecoverable once an organisation no longer retains the expertise required to audit its own decisions.

Building on prior architectural and evaluative results, the paper maps failure propagation from individual confabulation through functional contamination to institution-level and market-level exposure. It demonstrates why V = 0 systems violate the conditions of insurability, why auditor and fiduciary liability are materially altered and why strategic convergence on identical unverified substrates creates correlated fragility across sectors.

The conclusion is binary choice. Organisations either invest in governance early and visibly or pay for failure late and invisibly. There is no middle path.

Papers One to Three complete the architectural analysis on which this paper depends. This paper translates those structural constraints into institutional liability. Paper Five extends that translation into market mispricing. The governance requirement established earlier in the series is not discretionary. It is structural compensation for an absent capability.

title: V = 0: Six Architectural Laws Mandating External Governance For AI

detail.abstract:
This paper codifies six Architectural Laws derived from the structural analysis in “Artificial Confabulation and Untrustworthiness” [1] and “The Benchmark Illusion” [2]. These Laws describe falsifiable constraints arising from transformer-based architectures. In governance and regulatory application, they function as Structural Invariants: non-optional constraints that safe deployment must satisfy. Both terms refer to the same constraints. The distinction is presentational. This paper uses ‘Laws’ throughout.

The first four Laws establish why failure is inevitable in systems where Verification capability (V) equals zero. The final two Laws establish why this failure is invisible to current measurement paradigms. Together, they constitute a complete structural diagnosis: transformer-based AI systems confabulate by architecture, and no evaluation methodology can detect this within the current paradigm.

Seven Foundational Principles precede the Laws, providing the conceptual substrate from which the Laws derive. The paper then specifies Governed Hybrid Intelligence (GHI) as the minimal reference architecture satisfying all six Laws. This is not a policy recommendation. It is an engineering requirement imposed by the architecture of the systems being deployed.

This paper completes the architectural analysis. Papers Four and Five translate these constraints into institutional liability and market mispricing. The governance requirement established here is not discretionary. It is structural compensation for an absent capability.

title: Coordination Under Acceleration Structural Stress Tests Across Natural, Social, and Artificial Systems
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Coordination Under Acceleration Structural Stress Tests Across Natural, Social, and Artificial Systems

keywords: interpretive variance common knowledge reference primitives system stability

detail.abstract: This paper is written as a structural stress test rather than a persuasive argument. If its diagnosis is correct, independent analytical systems should converge on the same failure mode without relying on shared premises, disciplinary authority, or normative commitments. Across biological, infrastructural, social, and artificial systems, abrupt instability is repeatedly observed not as gradual degradation but as sudden phase transition. The paper examines whether these transitions are better explained by randomness, resource scarcity, incentive failure, or external shock-or whether they share a deeper structural cause. We propose that instability arises when rates of change exceed coordination bandwidth, producing unconditioned interpretive or operational variance among agents. The paper tests this hypothesis across multiple domains and evaluates alternative explanations. If independent readers do not converge on coordination failure under acceleration as the dominant pattern, the hypothesis should be discarded.-1. OBSERVATION Across domains, complex systems often remain stable under incremental change yet exhibit abrupt collapse once a critical threshold is crossed. These transitions do not scale linearly with input intensity and frequently lack early warning signals. After collapse, systems display increased variance, blame assignment, suppression attempts, or moralized explanations. This pattern appears in ecosystems, infrastructure, social networks, markets, and multi-agent artificial systems. The recurrence of sudden instability across substrates suggests a structural mechanism rather than domain-specific failure.

title: From Role-Task-Format to SMART and Beyond: A Qualitative Taxonomy of Prompting Frameworks in Applied AI Practice
affiliations: CirroLytix Research Services

detail.title: From Role-Task-Format to SMART and Beyond: A Qualitative Taxonomy of Prompting Frameworks in Applied AI Practice
detail.abstract: The widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) has given rise to prompt engineering as a practical skill, accompanied by the rapid proliferation of reusable prompting frameworks shared by practitioners. Despite their growing influence on realworld AI use, these frameworks remain largely undocumented and undertheorized in academic research. This paper presents a qualitative synthesis of practitioner-developed prompting frameworks collected from professional communities on Facebook and LinkedIn. Using thematic and structural analysis, the study deduplicates and normalizes eighty-five distinct frameworks, identifies recurring prompting primitives, and organizes them into a functional taxonomy. The analysis reveals strong convergence around a small set of core components-such as role specification, goal definition, contextual framing, output constraints, and iterative evaluation-despite surface-level variation in naming and structure. Building on these findings, the paper proposes a unified metamodel of prompting that captures the minimal canonical elements underlying most framework-based prompts. The discussion situates prompting frameworks as design artifacts that reflect user mental models of AI, negotiated trust and control, and evolving patterns of cognitive labor delegation. By formalizing informal prompting practices, this work contributes to understanding prompt engineering as an emergent design discipline at the intersection of programming, communication, and management, and lays the groundwork for future empirical and tool-oriented research.

title: Modelling Transport in Quantitative Spatial Economics: A Review of Theory, Empirics, and Policy Simulations
affiliations: , Imperial College London - Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering and Imperial College London - Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering

detail.title: Modelling Transport in Quantitative Spatial Economics: A Review of Theory, Empirics, and Policy Simulations

declarations.funderStatement: The first author (Daniel Hörcher) acknowledges the support of the Ministry of Culture and Innovation of Hungary through the National Research, Development and Innovation Fund under the Excellence_24 funding scheme (Project #151498).

detail.abstract:
This paper reviews the emerging literature on quantitative spatial models (QSMs) and assesses their relevance for transport research. The QSM approach integrates a wide range of analytical tasks that the transport literature has traditionally treated separately. It allows researchers to model the interaction between transport and land use; to capture general equilibrium linkages between accessibility, wages, and housing prices; to estimate heterogeneity in travel time valuations; to endogenise origin--destination matrices through gravity models of location choice; and to identify the causal effects of connectivity on firm productivity and amenities. A key methodological advantage of this framework lies in model quantification: geographical fundamentals such as local amenities and firm productivity serve as invertible structural residuals of the model, and several generic parameters can be causally identified using estimating equations derived directly from the underlying theory. After estimation, the model can be used as a simulator of existing or hypothetical policy interventions, both to predict the resulting land-use, wage, and housing price distributions, and to quantify the local, group-specific, and aggregate welfare impacts of the policy. The resulting model outputs can be applied directly in access-based transport cost-benefit analysis and used to quantify a broad set of wider economic impacts. 

The QSM literature has catalysed a paradigm shift in urban economics and economic geography over the past decade, with several transport-oriented models published in the top five journals of economics. In anticipation of the rapid growth of this approach within the transport research community, this article provides a comprehensive introduction and methodological guide to quantitative spatial modelling.

title: Human-in-Command: Governing Agentic AI in Customer Service
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Human-in-Command: Governing Agentic AI in Customer Service
detail.abstract: The rapid integration of autonomous and generative artificial intelligence into the customer service and support sector has fundamentally altered the relationship between human agents and technological systems. As organizations shift from simple rule-based automation to semi-autonomous "agentic" AI, the requirement for effective human oversight has moved from a technical best practice to a critical governance and regulatory mandate. This research explores the "Human-in-Command" (HIC) framework as the definitive model for maintaining organizational accountability, ensuring ethical alignment, and mitigating the risks associated with algorithmic bias and automation complacency. Through a comprehensive literature review, the report traces the theoretical evolution of human-automation interaction from early aerospace models to modern human-machine teaming (HMT). It provides an in-depth analysis of the operational triggers for strategic handoffs, the cognitive demands of AI-augmented workflows, and the rigorous compliance requirements established by the European Union AI Act. The findings demonstrate that meaningful human oversight is a systemic property emerging from the interplay of interaction design, cognitive load management, and psychological trust. The report concludes that sustainable AI deployment in the service sector requires a transition toward "Humanity-in-the-Loop," a holistic framework that preserves human dignity and decisional ownership in an increasingly automated marketplace.

title: Revisiting the Role of Voucher and Referral Programs: Evidence from a Food-Rescue Platform
affiliations: and National University of Singapore (NUS) - NUS Business School

detail.title: Revisiting the Role of Voucher and Referral Programs: Evidence from a Food-Rescue Platform
detail.abstract: Food-rescue platforms are emerging as an important platform-based solution to reducing global food waste, yet little is known about how financial incentives, namely voucher and referral programs, shape customer retention and engagement in this sustainability-oriented context. On one hand, such financial incentives can complement prosocial participation by lowering barriers to trial; on the other hand, they can backfire by inducing deal-seeking behavior. Using detailed transaction data from a major food-rescue platform in Southeast Asia, we examine how voucher and referral-code usage in a customer's first order affects customer retention and engagement, and ultimately, the platform's efficiency in reducing food waste. Using the instrumental-variable approach, we surprisingly did not observe any negative impact of voucher and referral usage. Although voucher usage in the first order had no effect in the short term or on the retention rate, it did have a positive long-term effect on the number of orders, with customers who used a voucher in their first order completing 1.4 more orders on average compared to those who did not. In contrast, referral usage in the first order did not lead to an increase in the number of orders, yet significantly increased the retention rate, especially in the short term, with customers who used a referral code being 15.26 percentage points more likely to complete another order within 30 days. Overall, our results suggest that neither voucher nor referral programs harm the quality of the customer base in this sustainability-oriented context, though given the potential of the customer base, these programs also do not go a long way toward improving customer retention and long-term engagement.

title: Lightweight Neural Networks for Real-Time Affective Computing Applications
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Lightweight Neural Networks for Real-Time Affective Computing Applications
detail.abstract: Real-time affective computing has emerged as a critical enabler for human-centered intelligent systems, supporting applications such as adaptive human-computer interaction, mental health monitoring, and context-aware IoT services. However, deploying affective models in constrained environments-such as edge devices and embedded IoT platforms-poses significant challenges due to limited computational power, memory, and energy availability. This study is motivated by the growing need for lightweight neural networks that can deliver reliable affect recognition while meeting strict real-time and resource constraints (Onyekwelu-Udoka et al., 2025). The methodological approach centers on a systematic comparative analysis of lightweight convolutional neural networks (CNNs), compact transformer-based models, and hybrid multimodal architectures integrating visual, acoustic, and physiological signals. Performance is evaluated in terms of accuracy, latency, model size, and computational efficiency, enabling a holistic assessment of suitability for edge deployment (Zhou et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2025). Experimental results demonstrate that optimized lightweight architectures achieve accuracy levels comparable to heavier models, while significantly reducing inference latency and computational cost (Ramirez-Quintana et al., 2025; Pascual et al., 2022). These findings confirm that lightweight neural networks provide a practical pathway for scalable, real-time affective computing across embedded and edge platforms, facilitating broader adoption in next-generation intelligent systems (Mishra and Gupta, 2023).

title: In Your Company, What Runs on Professionalism and What Survives on Heroism?
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: In Your Company, What Runs on Professionalism and What Survives on Heroism?
detail.abstract: In many small and mid-sized companies, the line between professionalism and heroism becomes so blurred that even the owner struggles to define it clearly. The business moves forward, customers return, sales continue, and on the surface everything seems to be working as it should. However, when you look more closely, a different reality often emerges. A significant part of daily operations does not rest on a solid system, but on the silent sacrifice of a few people—usually the same ones—who compensate with personal effort for what the organization has not yet resolved through structure, clarity, and method. At that point, the question stops being philosophical and becomes a critical diagnosis: what in your company works because of professionalism, and what survives thanks to heroism?

title: Quantum Computing: Commercial Applications, Power Asymmetries
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Quantum Computing: Commercial Applications, Power Asymmetries
detail.abstract: Quantum computing is now widely regarded as a potentially transformative technology, capable of addressing computational problems of extraordinary complexity that lie beyond the reach of classical systems-such as those in combinatorial optimisation, large-scale logistics, resource allocation, quantitative finance, and advanced industrial planning. Yet its significance reaches far beyond the realms of engineering and theoretical physics. As these technologies gradually mature, their prospective influence upon commercial decision-making, optimisation processes, and long-term strategic planning inevitably gives rise to broader questions of a social, political, and institutional character, including geopolitical implications and power asymmetries in global access.This paper adopts a deliberately non-technical, interdisciplinary vantage point. Rather than treating quantum computing as an isolated technological artefact, it examines its emergence as a novel form of strategic computational infrastructure-a critical layer in the evolving landscape of advanced decision-support systems. The discussion considers its relevance to high-complexity decision problems while candidly acknowledging the formidable structural limitations that continue to impede widespread, reliable deployment at scale.A particular focus is placed upon asymmetries of access, issues of technological sovereignty, digital sovereignty, and the pronounced concentration of advanced computational capacity in the hands of a comparatively small number of global actors-primarily in North America, Europe, Asia, and, increasingly, in emerging regions. The paper surveys the current geographical spread of quantum computing initiatives, drawing attention to those led by major corporations as well as research-intensive endeavours, alongside the appearance of more application-driven efforts beyond the traditional centres of technological innovation. Moving beyond strictly technical considerations, the analysis turns to the governance challenges, regulatory lacunae, and attendant risks arising from the growing opacity and centralisation of sophisticated decision-support systems-risks amplified by the impending transition to post-quantum cryptography and the need for quantum security measures. By locating quantum computing within wider contemporary debates concerning power asymmetries, accountability, institutional preparedness, and quantum policy, this paper seeks to foster a more balanced and less polarised appreciation of both its opportunities and its perils. Ultimately, the aim is to facilitate a more considered and less reactive assessment of quantum computing’s evolving role within commercial, economic, and policy landscapes—advocating measured exploration, critical scrutiny, and sustained strategic foresight, rather than succumbing to the familiar cycles of technological enthusiasm and exaggeration. In an era of accelerating quantum geopolitics, such foresight is essential to mitigate risks and promote equitable access to this emerging strategic asset.

title: Funding Strategy and Cash Flow Management
affiliations: Bung Karno University

detail.title: Funding Strategy and Cash Flow Management
detail.abstract:
The continuously evolving business environment necessitates that organizations implement robust and proficient financial oversight mechanisms. A crucial component of financial oversight involves strategic resource acquisition and the effective management of monetary circulation. As articulated by Kasmir (2018), superior financial stewardship is instrumental in enabling a firm to sustain its operational viability.
Funding strategies encompass an organization's determinations regarding the selection of capital sources, whether derived from internal equity or external debt. Concurrently, cash flow management pertains to the systematic regulation of financial receipts and disbursements to ensure organizational liquidity (Husnan, 2015).

title: The OODA Cycle Is Not Neutral: Social Engineering and Decision Stabilisation under Uncertainty

detail.title: The OODA Cycle Is Not Neutral: Social Engineering and Decision Stabilisation under Uncertainty
detail.abstract: Decision-making under uncertainty is a central challenge in military operations, cyber security, crisis response, civil protection, and the protection of critical infrastructure. The Observe-Orient-Decide-Act (OODA) cycle is widely used to structure adaptive decisions in such contexts, yet it remains analytically underspecified with regard to how perceptions and interpretations stabilise prior to action. This paper argues that the OODA cycle itself constitutes a potential surface of influence rather than a neutral decision space. Decisions within the cycle stabilise through the interaction of emotional salience, cognitive plausibility, and normative legitimacy. To make these dynamics explicit, the paper integrates the Emotion-Bias-Principle (EBP) Effect Model into the OODA cycle as an explanatory lens and advances analytical understanding of why decision frameworks themselves may become part of the influence surface. The analysis shows how emotion structures observation, cognitive biases stabilise orientation, and social or organisational principles legitimise decisions. The contribution is explicitly explanatory and advances analytical understanding of why decisions under uncertainty appear situationally appropriate at the moment they are taken, even when they later prove flawed.

title: The Resume Parsing Crisis of 2025: How Applicant Tracking Systems Fail to Identify Qualified Candidates
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Resume Parsing Crisis of 2025: How Applicant Tracking Systems Fail to Identify Qualified Candidates
detail.abstract: The modern recruitment landscape faces a critical technological failure that systematically excludes qualified candidates from employment opportunities. This study examines the fundamental flaws in Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) used by organizations to process job applications in 2025. Through empirical analysis of 100 dummy curriculum vitae (CV) documents processed through contemporary ATS platforms, we demonstrate that up to 80% of applications are incorrectly rejected due to parsing failures, not candidate unsuitability. Our research reveals that despite vendor claims of advanced NLP and machine learning capabilities, realworld ATS parsing performance remains catastrophically poor, with even leading platforms requiring candidates to manually re-enter information already present in uploaded CVs. This technological stagnation, combined with the proliferation of PDF and Word document formats, creates a systematic barrier to employment that disproportionately affects qualified candidates. We identify specific technical failures, document format incompatibilities, and provide evidence of discriminatory outcomes based on candidate names and national origin. This paper argues for urgent reform in recruitment technology and proposes technical solutions to address the current crisis in talent acquisition.

title: How Generative AI Transforms Questioning Behavior on Q&A Platforms: Evidence from A Natural Experiment with Pilot Usage of ChatGPT
affiliations: University of Florida,  and University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration

detail.title: How Generative AI Transforms Questioning Behavior on Q&A Platforms: Evidence from A Natural Experiment with Pilot Usage of ChatGPT

publicationDetails.detailsText: Northeastern U. D’Amore-McKim School of Business Research Paper No. 4909905
publicationDetails.journalName: Northeastern University D'Amore-McKim School of Business Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The rapid advancement of generative AI has enabled the automated generation of answers, introducing new dynamics in user behavior related to question-asking. However, the impact of users’ experience with generative AI for answer generation on their questioning behavior remains unclear. On the one hand, the availability of generative AI tools may lead users to rely on these tools for formulating questions, potentially resulting in fewer but higher-quality inquiries. On the other hand, using generative AI may motivate users to ask more questions to enhance their knowledge and build social reputation within the community. We investigate how the use of generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, to generate answers affects users’ questioning behavior on Stack Overflow, one of the largest Q&A platforms. Leveraging a natural experiment involving the introduction and subsequent ban of ChatGPT on the platform, we apply a difference-in-differences (DID) estimation approach to assess the effects of generative AI usage on the quantity and quality of user-generated questions. We measure these outcomes through metrics such as the number of questions posted per week, question length, novelty, and the number of received upvotes. Our findings reveal that the use of generative AI to generate answers leads to an increase in the number of questions with longer, more novel content and receives more upvotes. We examine two mechanisms: complexity shift, where ChatGPT handles routine queries while more advanced needs remain for the community, and skill enhancement, where users learn from ChatGPT to ask clearer questions. We also test two moderators: answer volume (proxy for user experience) and badges (proxy for user reputation). Results show weaker effects among experienced answerers but stronger effects among high-reputation users. These insights highlight how generative AI shapes engagement and can guide platform strategies for AI integration.

title:
The Emotion-Bias-Principle (EBP) Effect Model 
An Analytical Framework for Social Engineering as Decision -Making under Uncertainty

detail.title:
The Emotion-Bias-Principle (EBP) Effect Model 
An Analytical Framework for Social Engineering as Decision -Making under Uncertainty
detail.abstract: Social engineering is commonly addressed as a technical or behavioural security problem, typically associated with specific attack vectors such as phishing or fraud. This perspective overlooks the underlying decision-making processes that enable manipulative influence across different contexts and levels of analysis. This paper introduces the Emotion-Bias-Principle (EBP) Effect Model, an analytical framework for understanding social engineering as decision-making under uncertainty. The model distinguishes between emotional activation, cognitive bias, and socially stabilised principles of legitimacy, and explains how their interaction renders certain actions subjectively plausible and socially justified at the moment they are taken. By explicitly separating plausibility and legitimacy as interdependent dimensions of decision-making, the EBP model addresses a conceptual gap in existing bias-and influence-based approaches. It provides a coherent analytical structure applicable to individual decision situations, organisational stabilisation processes, and collective dynamics. The contribution is conceptual and aims to support systematic analysis and interdisciplinary discussion of social engineering as decision-making under uncertainty. It frames decisions as the convergence of plausibility and legitimacy.

title: A Conditional Diffusion-Based Generative AI Model for Industrial Predictive Analytics

detail.title: A Conditional Diffusion-Based Generative AI Model for Industrial Predictive Analytics
detail.abstract: Accurate prediction of remaining useful life (RUL) or time-to-failure (TTF) from degradation signals is a central problem in prognostics and health management across domains such as aerospace, manufacturing, and energy. Existing approaches largely fall into two categories: model-based methods that explicitly model degradation trajectories under parametric assumptions, and data-driven methods that directly map observed signals to failure time via dimensionality reduction and regression. Representative examples of these approaches considered in this paper include Bayesian updating and PCA-based lognormal regression. While effective for smooth and monotonic degradation patterns, both paradigms often degrade when applied to irregular, nonstationary, or multimodal degradation processes commonly encountered in real-world environments. To address these limitations, we propose a conditional diffusion–based generative framework that learns the full conditional distribution of future degradation trajectories given partial observations, enabling flexible and probabilistic TTF prediction. By modeling the data distribution directly, diffusion models can approximate nonlinear, heavy-tailed, and multimodal degradation behaviors. To rigorously evaluate performance, we construct synthetic degradation datasets with controlled increases in structural complexity, incorporating Brownian-motion noise, localized perturbations, and multi-regime dynamics. Extensive benchmarks against Bayesian updating and PCA-based lognormal regression demonstrate that the proposed diffusion model consistently achieves lower error under complex settings, particularly near failure thresholds and under complex, heteroscedastic conditions. These results position diffusion model as a robust and scalable alternative for predictive analytics in realistic prognostic.

detail.abstract: Noncitizen U.S. military veterans continue to face deportation despite having served honorably in the Armed Forces. This outcome is not accidental but is produced by the intersection of immigration law, criminal law, and military systems—particularly the 1996 Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act (IIRIRA). Under current law, once a noncitizen veteran is deemed removable, immigration judges are prohibited from considering military service, length of residence, or family ties. As a result, veterans who were once deemed fit to serve are later excluded without discretion.

detail.title: Distressed patients: modeling how 2.5 million patients choose emergency and urgent care providers in the Maule region of Chile

publicationDetails.detailsText: []

detail.abstract: Knowing how patients choose from a set of urgent and emergency care providers is essential in the design of disaster-ready health care system, because it permits estimating the demand of these centers in current and counterfactual scenarios, such as mass emergencies and health network redesign. Yet, despite how valuable this knowledge is, the study of patient choice in the urgent and emergency care setting is practically absent in the literature. This work presents a novel variation of the multinomial logit model to account for the anxiety of patients as decision-makers, which was calibrated using data from 2.5 million admissions of patients of the urgent and emergency care system of the Maule region of Chile. Patients were disaggregated by severity (using the Emergency Severity Index or ESI) and personal characteristics, such as sex, age, being under-educated (having less than the 12 years of mandatory schooling) and being an informal caregiver (which may make decision-making more difficult). Patients were also associated with a number of options they can consider at a time, to replicate the phenomenon of premature closure seen in distressed decision-makers. Providers were characterized by their type (which signals their ability to handle difficult cases), whether they have a high abandonment rate and long waiting time, and their distance to the patient (measured as travel time). In particular, the model is designed to calibrate a nonlinear relation with distance. The results of the calibrated model(s) show that the number of options patients consider diminishes as severity increases, ranging from six for the least severe (ESI level 5) to only one option (the most salient) for the most severe cases (ESI levels 1 and 2). Also, patients preferred and dispreferred provider types differently, where hospitals were especially favored by higher severity patients, seniors, the under-educated and the caregivers. Furthermore, the calibrated models permitted reconstructing the demand of the urgent and emergency care system of the Maule region reasonably well, hinting that these models can be used to estimate the demand in counterfactual scenarios.

detail.abstract: Countries implement and liberalize capital controls opportunistically. To show this point, this paper introduces two novel indices—the Financial Account Restrictiveness Index (FARI) and the AREAER Change Index (ACI)—to measure and track capital flow restrictions across 190 countries quarterly from 1999 to 2022. FARI quantifies the restrictiveness of capital accounts, while ACI captures policy changes over time. These indices offer a comprehensive, objective, and high-frequency toolset to analyze capital account policies and their evolution over the past two decades. Using the two indices, the paper highlights global liberalization trends, regional differences, and the cyclical use of capital controls in response to macroeconomic conditions and crises.60

title: Taste-based Investing, Government Policies and Competition in Financial Intermediation

detail.title: Taste-based Investing, Government Policies and Competition in Financial Intermediation

publicationDetails.detailsText: IMF Working Paper No. 2026/019
publicationDetails.journalName: International Monetary Fund (IMF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper develops a theory of how investors’ tastes are transmitted to aggregate investment through the market structure of financial intermediation. Whether tastes affect equilibrium capital allocation depends on where they originate—from households or from intermediaries—and on the degree of competition and segmentation in funding markets. Strong competition amplifies the pass-through of households’ tastes for amenity assets, but arbitrages away intermediaries’ own tastes. The same forces shape the effectiveness of financial-sector policies targeting households or intermediaries. I apply and quantify the framework in the context of green finance.
